rc.e: The clubs “mounted a campaign they called Good Roads,” and the next sentence lists the doing of it: printing pamphlets, mapping stretches, asking legislatures for money. Climbing up onto something is the meaning a reader expects in a passage full of bicycles, but no one climbs onto a campaign. Strategy: let the sentence after the word show which meaning is at work.

rc.q: The sentence “The argument changed when the mail changed” mainly serves to
c: list all of the printed pamphlets and route maps that the cycling clubs produced.
repeat the farmers' objection about taxes and city sportsmen in different words.
explain the way the mail had been carried to farm families in earlier centuries.
mark the point after which paving was no longer dismissed as a favor to city riders.
rc.e: It stands between the farmers' complaint about city sportsmen and the counties that suddenly began to build, so it announces a switch in reasons. The choice about repeating the objection misses that the sentence overturns the complaint rather than restating it. Strategy: a short sentence set between longer passages usually marks a turn.

rc.q: In the last sentence, saying that drivers “owed a debt to people who had been pedaling” means that
c: the author wishes that automobiles had never replaced bicycles at all.
drivers benefited from work that cyclists had done for reasons of their own.
drivers should have repaid the old cycling clubs with money of their own.
cyclists handled the early automobiles better than other people did.
rc.e: No payment appears anywhere in the passage; the debt is figurative, naming a benefit drivers received from a campaign fought for bicycles. The choice about repaying the clubs with money takes the figure of speech literally, which is the usual trap in this kind of item. Strategy: ask what an image stands for before accepting its literal sense.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A bird's color depends on the food that the bird eats.
A feather's color disappears once the feather is crushed.
Each branch of a feather holds a layer of keratin.
A jay's blue comes from structure, not from a pigment.
rc.e: The passage opens by showing that grinding a jay's feather takes the blue away, explains that the color comes from the spacing of air pockets, and closes by saying the jay makes its blue rather than carrying it. Saying a bird's color comes from its food describes only the cardinal, which the passage brings in to contrast with the jay. Strategy: the main idea has to hold true for the beginning and the ending, not just one example in the middle.

y.A: That is how the cardinal's red is made, and the passage offers it as the opposite case to the jay, not as the rule for both birds.
y.B: The red feather ground to powder leaves red dust, so crushing a feather does not take every color away — only a color that depends on an arrangement can be crushed out of one.
y.C: The passage does say this, which is why it feels familiar, but it is one small piece of the explanation rather than the point the whole passage is making.

rc.q: According to the passage, what happens when a red feather is ground into powder?
c: The dust turns a dull brown, as the jay's did.
The dust left in the palm is still red.
The dust keeps a faint trace of pink.
The dust looks red at certain angles.
rc.e: The third paragraph states that a red feather ground to powder leaves red dust in the palm, because the color is a pigment and a pigment is a thing you can hold. The dull brown dust belongs to the jay's feather in the first paragraph. Strategy: check which bird the detail belongs to before you pick it.

y.A: Dull brown dust is what the jay's feather leaves behind, and the passage brings the red feather in precisely because it behaves differently.
y.C: The passage calls the dust red, with nothing to suggest the color weakens when the feather is ground.
y.D: No angle is mentioned for the dust; the passage's second test is about light coming through from behind, not about where a viewer stands.

rc.q: A feather from an unfamiliar bird is ground to powder, and the powder is still orange. The passage best supports concluding that
c: the feather held air pockets arranged inside it.
the orange came from a pigment in the feather.
the bird eats the same food a cardinal eats.
light from behind would turn the feather brown.
rc.e: The passage sets up a test: a color made by an arrangement disappears when the arrangement is crushed, while a color made by pigment survives, as the red dust does. Orange powder that keeps its color therefore behaves like the cardinal's red and must be a pigment. Strategy: when a question gives you a new case, apply the rule the passage demonstrated rather than looking for the new case in the text.

y.A: Arranged air pockets make a color that lasts only as long as the arrangement does, so a color that survives grinding points away from this answer.
y.C: The passage says a bird builds a pigment from what it eats, but it never says that one pigment means one particular diet.
y.D: Turning brown in light from behind is the jay's result, and this feather has just behaved like the cardinal's, which stays its own color when it is lit that way.

rc.q: In the second paragraph, *swallows* most nearly means
c: darts and dives like a small bird.
swiftly eats a bite of food.
takes it in and absorbs it.
sends it straight back to the eye.
rc.e: The sentence before says the red and yellow light travels deeper into the feather, and it never comes back out, so the dark pigment takes it in. The bird meaning is planted by the subject matter, which is exactly why it is worth testing inside the sentence. Strategy: read the sentence before the word to see what the word is actually doing there.

y.A: A swallow is a bird, and the word is planted in a passage about birds, but here it names what a layer of dark pigment does, and a layer of pigment is not a creature.
y.B: This is the everyday meaning, and a layer of pigment does not eat anything; what reaches it is light.
y.D: Sending light back toward the eye is what the air pockets do with blue, and it is the opposite of what happens to the light that travels deeper in.

rc.q: The paragraph beginning "A cardinal's red works the other way" mainly serves to
c: set a true pigment beside the jay's kind of blue.
give one more example of color made by structure.
explain why the cardinal's red is the brighter color.
teach a reader how to test a feather at home.
rc.e: The paragraph begins by saying the cardinal's red works the other way, then describes two tests that come out differently for a pigment and for an arrangement. Its job is comparison, which is why the word other is doing so much work in its first sentence. Strategy: watch the opening sentence of a paragraph for a signal about what the paragraph is for.

y.B: The cardinal's red is a pigment, which is the other kind of color entirely, so this paragraph adds a contrast rather than another example.
y.C: The passage never compares how bright the two colors are; it compares how each one is made.
y.D: Two tests are described, but they are there to show that the two colors behave differently, not to hand a reader a procedure to carry out.

rc.q: In the last two sentences, saying that the jay does not carry its blue but makes it suggests that
c: the color happens when light meets the structure.
the jay can change its feathers' color at will.
the feather works to keep its blue from fading.
the feather would be blue even in the dark.
rc.e: The closing lines draw a line between having a color, the way the cardinal has a pigment you can hold, and making one, which happens only when light strikes the arranged pockets and comes back. Reading makes as effort or as choice turns a figure of speech into a literal claim the passage does not make. Strategy: ask what an author's phrase is contrasted with before deciding what it means.

y.B: The bird is not choosing anything here; makes describes the feather's structure at work, not a decision the jay takes.
y.C: This takes makes to mean effort, and no fading and no effort appear anywhere in the passage.
y.D: The sentence says the blue arrives with the light, and the paragraph before says the blue depends on light bouncing back off a structure.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A tree's rings record each year's weather, and that record can date old wood.
Counting a tree's rings is the surest way to learn how old the tree really is.
Trees growing in warm, wet places are of little use to researchers.
A wide ring proves that one tree was healthier than the trees near it.
rc.e: The passage grants that counting rings gives an age, calls that the least interesting thing they can tell you, and then spends two paragraphs on what the widths record and how that record dates a beam from an old roof. The choice about counting for age stops where the first paragraph stops. Strategy: when a passage calls an idea the least interesting thing, the main idea is what comes after it.

y.B: Counting for age is the one use the passage grants and then sets aside as the least interesting thing the rings can tell you, and the last paragraph shows a count can even be off by a year.
y.C: Those trees are one limit named near the end, not what the passage as a whole is about.
y.D: A wide ring is tied to a wet, mild year, not to one tree doing better than its neighbours.

rc.q: According to the passage, the ring a reader sees is the line between
c: the pale spring wood and the dark wood of that year.
one year's dark wood and next spring's pale wood.
the bark of the tree and the new wood beneath it.
the wood of a wet year and the wood of a dry year.
rc.e: The second paragraph names the line outright: the ring you see is where one year's dark wood stops and next spring's pale wood begins. The pale-and-dark pair inside one year is a real boundary but not the one the passage points at, and the new layer of wood goes beneath the bark rather than on it. Strategy: find the sentence that defines the thing and read it exactly.

y.A: Those two do sit side by side within a single year, but the passage points at the other edge — where one year's dark wood stops and the next spring's pale wood begins.
y.C: The tree adds its new layer of wood beneath the bark, so the bark is not the edge being described.
y.D: Wet and dry years give wide and narrow rings, but the line itself is a change from dark wood to pale wood, not a border between two kinds of year.

rc.q: The passage suggests that the researcher could not date the beam without
c: a mark left on the beam by whoever built the roof.
a count of how many rings the beam still holds.
rings from trees whose years are already known.
a sample taken from the same roof's other beams.
rc.e: A living tree's outermost ring is this year's, so its rings can be counted back to real years; the beam is dated by sliding its own pattern along that record until the wide and narrow years line up. Without a set of rings whose years are already settled, the beam's pattern is just a pattern with nowhere to sit. Strategy: ask what a method borrows from outside the object it is examining.

y.A: The passage says the beam is dated though nobody wrote a date on it, so a written mark is exactly what is missing.
y.B: Counting tells you how many years the wood grew, not which years those were.
y.D: The pattern is slid along the record kept by living trees, and other beams from the same roof would carry no known years of their own.

rc.q: In the third paragraph, *agreement* most nearly means
c: a promise made between two people.
the same weather from year to year.
a rule about matching word forms.
rc.e: The sentence just before says the bands run in step, so the agreement named next is that matching between trees. The everyday promise-between-people meaning is the trap, and the weather choice lifts a true phrase from the sentence before and attaches the word to the wrong thing — what runs in step is the patterns. Strategy: put your choice into the sentence in place of the word and check that it still describes the same thing.

y.A: That is the word's everyday meaning, but nobody here is promising anything — what is happening is that bands are matching.
y.B: The sentence before does say trees in one region live through the same weather, but that agreement points back at the patterns running in step, and the passage's whole point is that the weather differs from year to year.
y.C: Agreement does mean that in a grammar lesson, where a subject and a verb must match, but this sentence is about bands of wood rather than words.

rc.q: The last paragraph mainly serves to
c: set out the limits of a method the passage has explained.
explain again how a tree lays down wood each spring.
argue that ring patterns are too unreliable to use.
explain how one beam is matched against the living record.
rc.e: The paragraph announces that the limits are the ordinary kind and then names them — no clear band where it is warm and wet all year, a skipped year, a doubled one — before closing with the safeguard of checking many trees. Saying ring patterns are too unreliable to use goes further than a paragraph that ends by explaining how researchers work around the trouble, and the matching of a beam to the living record has already happened a paragraph earlier. Strategy: a paragraph that names limits and then a safeguard is qualifying a method, not throwing it out.

y.B: That was settled in the second paragraph; the last one turns to where the method runs into trouble.
y.C: The paragraph raises problems and then closes with the safeguard of checking many trees, which is a caution rather than a rejection.
y.D: Matching a beam against the living record is the third paragraph's job; the last one is about where that matching cannot be trusted.

rc.q: The comparison in “the rings are a row of entries, one for every year the tree stood” suggests that the rings
c: are written by hand onto the wood.
keep a record, one year at a time.
are all exactly the same width.
grow larger each year of a tree's life.
rc.e: An entry is a line written in a record, and the passage sets the rings in order with one for every year the tree stood, so the comparison turns the trunk into a year-by-year log. Taking the picture literally, as writing on the wood, misses that a comparison borrows a quality rather than stating a fact. Strategy: with a comparison, ask which quality is being borrowed, not whether the picture is literally true.

y.A: The rings are compared to written entries, but nothing in the passage says anyone writes on the wood.
y.C: The passage says the opposite — wide in a wet, mild year and narrow in a dry, hard one.
y.D: Ring width depends on the weather of that year, not on how old the tree has become.

rc.q: What does the scene mainly show about Theo?
c: He realizes that his grandmother left him more work than he could manage.
He discovers that he is not suited to selling fruit at a busy market stall.
He gives up a rehearsed sales line and lets customers judge the fruit themselves.
He learns that neat handwriting matters far more than he had ever thought.
rc.e: Theo breaks off his practiced sentence, hands over a cherry instead of a description, and by four o’clock the crate is empty. The choice about neat handwriting reverses the ending, in which the hastily written, messier line is the one that works. Strategy: let the final sentence test your choice.

rc.q: What does Theo do to his price card after the woman buys the cherries?
c: He crosses out a line and adds new words in messier handwriting.
He copies the prices onto it from his grandmother’s own list.
He throws the card away and writes out a new one from scratch.
He props it up against the crate of plums at the end of the table.
rc.e: The last paragraph says he crossed out one line and wrote underneath “in handwriting that was not nearly as neat.” The choice about propping the card against the plums moves a real detail — the card propped against the scale — to the wrong moment in the scene. Strategy: watch where in the scene each detail happens.

rc.q: The bowl under the table was most likely put there so that
c: Theo could keep count of how many cherries he had sold.
Theo’s grandmother would have something to eat later on.
bruised cherries could be kept out of the customers’ sight.
customers could taste a cherry before buying.
rc.e: Theo assumes the bowl is her lunch, but it does its work the instant he offers a cherry to the woman, and he then sets it on the table “where people could reach it.” The lunch choice is what the character guesses, not what the scene shows. Strategy: trust what happens in a scene over what a character assumes.

rc.q: In the first paragraph, *mind* most nearly means
rc.e: His grandmother leaves and “for two hours the stall was his to mind,” so he is the one looking after it. Being bothered by something is the meaning most readers meet first, as in “I don’t mind,” but a stall cannot be bothered by anybody. Strategy: substitute each choice into the sentence and hear which one survives.

rc.q: The dash in “They’re excellent for—” marks the point at which
c: Theo abandons the sentence he practiced and changes his approach.
Theo’s grandmother comes back to the stall with the change.
the woman in the yellow coat interrupts Theo with another question.
Theo forgets the prices he had memorized before the market opened.
rc.e: The narrator says he stopped “because he could hear how it sounded: like a boy repeating something,” and from there he shows the fruit instead of describing it. The choice about an interruption gives the woman credit for a decision Theo makes on his own. Strategy: punctuation that breaks a sentence often marks the turn of a scene.

rc.q: The last sentence, about the empty crate and the beautifully arranged plums, is best described as
c: wistful and sad about the end of a long day at the market.
quietly amused, setting what looked good beside what actually sold.
excited and boastful about how much money Theo managed to earn.
sharply critical of the mistakes Theo made over the course of the day.
rc.e: The plums are called “arranged so beautifully” at the exact moment we learn they did not sell, a small joke the narrator makes without scolding Theo. Reading the line as sharp criticism mistakes gentle humor for blame. Strategy: notice when a detail from the opening returns with its meaning changed.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A damper is the only device that keeps a very tall tower standing up.
Strong wind is the greatest danger that any tall building will ever face.
A building that moves at all in the wind has been built incorrectly.
A tall building is built to sway a little and then stop quickly.
rc.e: The passage first explains why a frame is given room to bend and then why engineers work to make the motion fade fast, ending with what they actually measure. The choice naming the damper treats one device as the entire design and ignores the frame's give. Strategy: a main idea must hold both halves of a two-part explanation.

rc.q: According to the passage, where is a damper placed in a tower?
c: Inside the outer wall on every floor from top to bottom.
Beside the scale model inside the engineers' wind tunnel.
High in the building, on cables or on a slick steel surface.
Below the ground floor, deep inside the building's foundation.
rc.e: The third paragraph describes an enormous weight “hung high in the building on cables or resting on a slick steel surface.” The wind tunnel choice reuses the final paragraph, where models, not dampers, are placed. Strategy: reread the sentence that names the thing the question asks about.

rc.q: The passage suggests that a damper is added mainly to
c: make a building that is already safe feel steadier to the people inside.
keep the building from moving at all, even during the hardest storm.
make the steel frame far stiffer than it would otherwise have been.
lower the cost of putting up a tall tower in a crowded city.
rc.e: The paragraph says long swaying “feels alarming to the people inside it, even when it is perfectly safe,” and the damper is introduced as the answer to that problem. The choice about stopping all motion ignores “the sway fades in seconds instead of minutes,” which shortens the movement rather than ending it. Strategy: notice the exact problem a device is introduced to solve.

rc.q: In the second paragraph, *give* most nearly means
c: a willingness to share things with others.
a sudden collapse under a heavy weight.
a present that is offered without charge.
the ability to bend and spring back.
rc.e: The frame built with “a measured amount of give” bends, sheds the energy of the gust, and “returns to where it started.” The sudden-collapse choice is tempting because a beam can “give way,” but this frame comes back rather than failing. Strategy: read one sentence past the word before choosing.

rc.q: The sentence “The harder problem is not the leaning but the lingering” mainly serves to
c: give an example of a tall tower that was damaged in a winter storm.
shift the discussion from why buildings bend to how the motion stops.
introduce an objection that the author goes on to reject in detail.
restate the point of the opening paragraph in stronger, plainer language.
rc.e: Everything before it explains bending; everything after it explains the damper that shortens the sway. Calling it an objection fails, because the author agrees with the sentence and builds on it instead of answering it. Strategy: read the sentences on both sides to see what a hinge sentence separates.

rc.q: The last three sentences (“In a wind tunnel … how quickly it stops.”) create a tone of
c: doubt about whether wind tunnel tests are worth the trouble.
quiet confidence about what the engineers already know.
alarm at how far a tall building moves during a storm.
impatience with engineers who measure too many things.
rc.e: The short, flat sentences — “They already know it will” — present the movement as settled fact rather than a surprise or a worry. Alarm is the reaction the whole passage argues against, beginning with “it is not a flaw.” Strategy: read a passage's closing lines for the author's settled position.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Sawdust was the coldest material the workers in the ice trade could find.
Ice lasted the summer because the walls and the stacking both slowed heat.
Ships once carried ice from northern ponds to harbors in far warmer places.
Winters in the past were far colder than any winter people now know of.
rc.e: The passage says the icehouse made no cold of its own and was built only to slow heat down, and then spends two paragraphs on the two ways that was done: doubled walls packed with sawdust, and blocks cut large and stacked tight so little surface was left in the open. The choice about ships is a real detail from the last paragraph, but a detail cannot be the main idea. Strategy: pick the statement the middle paragraphs are busy proving, not the one that appears only once.

y.A: The passage says flatly that sawdust is not cold — its whole usefulness is that heat travels through it badly.
y.C: That is true, but it is one sentence near the end, not what the whole passage is built to explain.
y.D: The passage never compares old winters with modern ones; it only describes what people did with the ice a winter gave them.

rc.q: According to the passage, why did workers cut the ice into large blocks instead of small pieces?
c: A large block has less surface than the same ice in pieces.
Large blocks were easier for the crews to carry down a hill.
Small pieces would have melted before reaching the icehouse.
Large blocks sold for a higher price in the warm harbors.
rc.e: The third paragraph gives the reason directly: ice melts at its surface, and one large block has less surface, for the amount of ice in it, than the same ice chopped into pieces. Less exposed surface means slower melting, which is why workers also stacked the blocks tight and filled the seams. Strategy: when a paragraph states a rule and then a practice, the rule is the answer to "why".

y.B: The passage mentions hauling the blocks but never says the large size made carrying them any easier.
y.C: The passage does say the blocks were hauled some distance, but the reason it gives for cutting them large is about how slowly stored ice melts, not about the trip.
y.D: The passage says nothing about price — only about how quickly ice of different shapes melts.

rc.q: Based on the passage, which change would most likely make stored ice last longer?
c: Splitting the blocks into smaller pieces before they are stacked.
Packing a thicker layer of sawdust between the doubled walls.
Leaving wide gaps between the blocks so air can circulate.
Rinsing the blocks with cold water before stacking them.
rc.e: Sawdust is described as a poor path for heat, and the passage concludes that heat which cannot get in cannot melt anything, so a thicker packing in the wall cavity means less heat reaching the ice. The rinsing choice is the tempting one, because cold water sounds helpful; only the passage's own sentence about meltwater — it carries heat into the pile faster than still air could — rules it out. Strategy: apply the reason the passage gives for each practice to see whether a change helps it or fights it.

y.A: Smaller pieces have more surface for the same amount of ice, and surface is exactly what sets the pace of melting.
y.C: Workers did the opposite, stacking the blocks tight and filling the seams so little ice was left in the open.
y.D: Cold water sounds like it should help, but the passage says water lying against the ice carries heat into it faster than still air does.

rc.q: In the third paragraph, *standing* most nearly means
c: upright on its feet, not lying down.
waiting its turn in a line.
lasting on and on for years.
not draining away from a place.
rc.e: The rest of the same sentence explains the word: the floor was sloped, and a floor is sloped for water that would otherwise sit where it lands. Meltwater standing against the pile is meltwater that has not drained away, and that is the water the passage says carries heat into the ice. The upright sense is the one the word usually carries, which is what makes it the trap. Strategy: when a familiar word sits oddly, look for the detail in the same sentence that was built to deal with it — here, the slope.

y.A: That is the word's everyday meaning, but water has no feet; the sentence is about water that stays where it collects.
y.B: Nothing in the passage is queuing — the meltwater is not waiting for anything, it is sitting against the ice.
y.C: "Standing" can mean long-lasting, but this is meltwater running off a pile of ice, and the slope exists to get rid of it quickly.

rc.q: The sentence "The shape of the stack mattered too" tells the reader that the third paragraph will
c: add another reason the ice melted slowly.
repeat the point about sawdust in new words.
explain how ships reached the far-off harbors.
admit how much of each load melted anyway.
rc.e: The word "too" adds something to what came before: the second paragraph explained the building, and the third explains the ice, with exposed surface as one more thing that controlled melting. A paragraph that only restated the sawdust point would have no use for "too". Strategy: a small linking word like "too" or "also" usually announces that a new reason is being added to an old one.

y.B: The paragraph leaves the walls behind entirely and talks about the ice itself — its surface, its size, how it was stacked.
y.C: The ships do not appear until the paragraph after this one, and their voyage is not what "the stack" refers to.
y.D: The passage does admit that, but a paragraph later; this sentence is still introducing the ways melting was slowed.

rc.q: The last sentence, "It was a machine for making winter last," suggests that the icehouse
c: was powered by an engine that the workers ran.
made the winter season itself grow longer.
held on to winter's ice well into the summer.
was more useful in winter than in the summer.
rc.e: The passage sets the sentence against its opposite — the icehouse was never a machine for making cold — so what it makes is time: ice cut in January is still solid in August. Reading "machine" literally, as something with an engine, misses that the whole sentence is a figure of speech. Strategy: when a sentence says what something is *not* right before saying what it is, use the contrast to pin down the meaning.

y.A: "Machine" is being used as a figure of speech; the building described has walls, a door and a sloped floor, and no moving parts at all.
y.B: No building can stretch a season; what was stretched was the usefulness of one winter's ice.
y.D: The opening says the January work was for July, and the ice was still solid in August — the icehouse earned its keep in the warm months.

rc.q: What does the scene mainly show about Ines's job that evening?
c: It taught her to understand the talk as well as Rosa did.
It looked like nothing and demanded constant attention.
It was harder than she should have been asked to try.
It mattered far less to the talk than she had hoped.
rc.e: The first sentence calls it the easiest job in the hall, and everything after it is work — the failed plan, the red slash, the counting back, the thumb held in place until it wore a crease in the paper. The choice about understanding the talk is ruled out by the passage's own words that the typed words meant almost nothing to her. Strategy: when a story opens by calling something easy, read the rest as the answer to that claim.

y.A: The passage says the typed words "meant almost nothing to her" — she worked from the shapes on the page and the red slashes, not from following what her aunt was saying.
y.C: She finds the job hard and does it anyway; nothing in the passage suggests she was wrongly asked, and by the end she is managing it without looking down.
y.D: The story points the other way: each photograph had to land on the sentence that needed it, and the one that lands correctly is the moment her aunt can keep reading.

rc.q: According to the passage, how did Ines know when to change the picture?
c: She listened for the words just before each change.
She waited for a nod from her aunt across the room.
She counted the sentences as her aunt read them.
She watched Rosa's finger reach the red slash.
rc.e: The fourth paragraph gives the method in order: find the red slash, count back two lines, put a thumb there, get ready when the finger arrives at the thumb, and press when the finger arrives at the slash. Listening for the words is a real detail from the passage, but it is the plan she abandoned. Strategy: check whether a detail describes what the character tried or what actually worked.

y.A: That was her first plan, and the passage says it failed: by the time she heard those words, "they had gone past."
y.B: Rosa never signals her. The passage makes a point of saying Rosa did not glance over, which is why Ines has to find the cue herself.
y.C: The counting in the passage happens once, on paper — two lines back from a slash — and not as a running count through the talk.

rc.q: Ines treats her aunt's not glancing over as "the highest compliment available" most likely because it means
c: the picture had not needed changing on that line.
the picture came on time and did not interrupt Rosa.
Rosa was pleased with how the talk itself was going.
Rosa had forgotten that Ines was sitting nearby.
rc.e: A picture that arrived late or on the wrong sentence would force the speaker to look across and check, so a speaker who never looks across is a speaker who was never interrupted. Reading the line as forgetfulness mistakes being unnoticed for being unneeded, when the whole scene rests on how much Rosa needs her. Strategy: ask what would have happened instead if the character had done the job badly.

y.A: It did need changing, and it changed: the sentence just before says the photograph arrived on the word it belonged to.
y.C: Nothing in the passage reports what Rosa thought of her own talk; the sentence attaches her steadiness to the photograph landing correctly.
y.D: Rosa is depending on her for pictures she cannot change herself, and being forgotten would be no compliment at all.

rc.q: In "black clusters where the paragraphs were busy," *busy* most nearly means
rc.e: The second half of the same sentence gives the measure: the clusters are black where the paragraphs are busy and white where they thin out, so the word is describing how crowded the printing looks. The ordinary meaning about a person with too much to do is the one to test first and then reject, because a paragraph has no errands. Strategy: when a sentence sets two halves against each other, the second half often defines the first.

y.B: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but it describes a person with a lot to do, and a paragraph on a page has no work to be occupied with.
y.C: A busy street is noisy, but the sentence is about how a printed page looks to someone holding it, not about sound or motion.
y.D: This describes someone rushing about; the paragraphs in the passage are sitting still on a sheet of paper, differing only in how crowded they are.

rc.q: The three sentences beginning "You sat at a small table" mainly serve to
c: give the reader directions for running the pictures.
describe what the rest of the room did during the talk.
show the job as Ines pictured it before she tried it.
suggest that Ines had been talked into taking the job.
rc.e: The story steps out of Ines for three sentences to lay out the job the way she expected it, as though it were obvious to anybody — and then drops straight back with the line about her mistake. Everything after that is the same job from the inside: a finger to watch, a slash to find, a thumb to keep in place. Strategy: when a narrator changes who the sentences are about, ask what that change shows which the ordinary telling could not.

y.A: They instruct nobody. They restate what the job sounded like from outside, which is why the very next line calls it a mistake.
y.B: The room is not doing these things; sitting at the small table and pressing the button are Ines's own job, seen before she began it.
y.D: The first sentence says she agreed because of how the job sounded, and the passage never shows anyone persuading her.

rc.q: The comparison "She watched the way a person crossing a street watches" suggests that Ines
c: paid attention to what was coming, not what was here.
watched several things happening at the same time.
was frightened by the traffic on the road outside.
thought the room was as crowded as a busy street.
rc.e: Someone stepping off a kerb is not watching the empty road in front of them but the car that has not arrived yet, and the rest of the sentence spells the comparison out: ahead of herself, two lines early, her thumb already in place. Taking the street literally turns a figure of speech into a scene the story never has. Strategy: after a comparison, read the words that follow it — the author usually explains the image straight away.

y.B: A busy street is the first thing the word brings to mind, but the rest of the sentence is about being early rather than about watching a crowd.
y.C: There is no traffic in the story; the street is a comparison, not a place anyone goes.
y.D: The comparison is about how she watched, not about how full or noisy the hall was.

rc.q: The passage is mainly written to
c: prove that repairing a broken object always costs a school less money than replacing it with a new one.
describe the objects that the Thursday repair table at Fenwick Middle School brought back in its first term.
explain why building projects such as birdhouses and model bridges should be removed from schools entirely.
argue that schools should set aside regular time for repair, because repairing teaches careful attention.
rc.e: The author asks for “one bench, one box of tools, and one period a week for repair” and says the point of the hour “is to teach a habit of looking.” The choice about the Fenwick table names one supporting example, and the choice about saving money is contradicted by the author's own words that the point “is not to save the school money on chairs.” Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole argument, not one example.

rc.q: According to the passage, what did the Thursday repair table bring back during its first term?
c: Forty-one items, every one of them either a lamp or an umbrella.
Forty-one items, including eleven lamps and fifteen damaged library books.
Four items, one for each of the four students who stayed until June.
Fifteen backpacks and nine library books with badly broken spines.
rc.e: The passage lists forty-one items: eleven lamps, nine backpacks, six umbrellas, and fifteen library books with broken spines. The choice naming four items confuses the four long-term students with the count of objects, and the backpacks-and-books choice swaps those two numbers. Strategy: put your finger on the exact sentence before choosing.

rc.q: The author would most likely say that a school's repair period is working well when
c: the school spends far less money on new furniture than it did the year before.
every broken object brought to the bench is successfully fixed by a student.
students finish their repairs faster than a paid repair shop nearby would.
students keep coming back after the first excitement and show newcomers what they know.
rc.e: The author calls four the number worth watching — the students still at the table in June, “showing newcomers how to seat a screw” — so a lasting habit and passed-on skill are the real measure. The choice about furniture savings is ruled out by “not to save the school money,” and the choice about fixing everything by the admission that “some objects truly cannot be mended.” Strategy: infer from what the author calls important, not from what sounds sensible in general.

rc.q: As used in the second paragraph, “sound” most nearly means
rc.e: The sentence contrasts one loose leg with the rest of the chair, so the word describes the parts that are still whole and strong. Making a noise and sleeping deeply are the word's everyday meanings, and neither fits a chair being examined for damage. Strategy: read the whole sentence with each choice substituted in.

rc.q: What does the second paragraph do in the author's argument?
c: It offers the first evidence from a real school that a repair table can actually work.
It lists the tools and the supplies that a school repair bench would need to buy.
It states the objection the author hears most often, grants part of it, and then answers it.
It gives up the claim made in the first paragraph and proposes a completely different plan.
rc.e: The paragraph names the objection the author hears most often (repairing is slower), concedes “That is true,” and then answers it: “the objection mistakes what the period is for.” The choice about evidence from a real school describes the third paragraph, which is where Fenwick appears. Strategy: ask what job each paragraph does for the argument, not just what it mentions.

rc.q: In the last paragraph the author writes that the difficulty of repair “does not weaken the case; it sharpens it.” This shows that the author
c: turns a fact that seems to weaken the argument into a reason for it.
admits that the argument has finally been defeated by modern machines.
is unsure whether repair is really worth teaching to students after all.
is making a joke about how complicated modern machines have become.
rc.e: The author grants that machines are getting harder to open and that some things cannot be mended, then argues that scarcity makes the skill of judging what can be fixed more valuable, not less. The choices about defeat and uncertainty misread a confident closing as a retreat. Strategy: watch what an author does with a fact that seems unhelpful — a strong writer often puts it to work.

rc.q: The passage is mainly about
c: how ice on the Niagara River trapped a boy on the wrong side for eight long days.
how a group of engineers decided that a bridge across the Niagara Gorge could not be built.
how a boy's kite took the first line across the Niagara Gorge and made a bridge possible.
how suspension bridges are built in northern places with long, cold winters.
rc.e: The passage opens with the need for “one thin thread” to reach the far side and closes with a bridge standing “where a boy's kite string had gone first.” The eight days of ice are one episode inside that story, and the choice about engineers giving up contradicts the ending. Strategy: the main idea should match the first sentence and the last sentence at once.

rc.q: According to the passage, why did Homan Walsh cross to the Canadian side before flying his kite?
c: The rocky gorge was much narrower on the Canadian side than elsewhere.
The winter ferry did not run from the American rim at any time in January.
The wind in the gorge blew from the Canadian side toward the American side.
The five-dollar prize could only be claimed by someone standing on the Canadian rim.
rc.e: The passage states that the steady wind blew from the Canadian side toward the American side, so a kite launched from the American rim “would be carried away from the crossing.” The choices about a narrower gorge, the prize, and the ferry add reasons the passage never gives, and the walls are described as eight hundred feet apart with no narrow place mentioned. Strategy: a “why” question usually has its answer in the sentence right before or after the action.

rc.q: The passage suggests that Homan's real advantage over the other contestants was that he
c: had built a far stronger kite than anyone else who entered the contest.
had helped the engineers build several other bridges before this one.
was the only person the engineer in charge allowed to enter the contest.
worked out how the wind moved through the gorge and changed where he started.
rc.e: The passage says he “understood something the adults seem to have overlooked” and then explains the wind, which is why he ferried across before launching. The stronger-kite choice is unsupported — his kite had to be mended, not upgraded — and a contest open to “whoever” could do it rules out the choice about being the only entrant. Strategy: an inference must be built from details the passage actually supplies.

rc.q: As used in the third paragraph (“This time the string held”), “held” most nearly means
c: carried or grasped in the hands.
took place, as a meeting does.
rc.e: This flight is set against the earlier one, in which “the line snapped,” so the string this time stayed unbroken while the kite pulled on it. Carrying something in the hands is the first meaning most readers reach for, but nobody is holding the string in that sentence. Strategy: when a familiar word turns up in an odd place, find the sentence it answers and let that decide the meaning.

rc.q: The last paragraph mainly serves to
c: list the goods that the ferries carried back and forth across the Niagara River.
argue that public contests are the best way to solve difficult engineering problems.
describe in detail how Homan found his kite on the far bank and then repaired it.
show how a string too weak to hold real weight became a cable strong enough for a bridge.
rc.e: The paragraph moves from string to cord to rope to cable, showing how the smallest beginning grew into the bridge. Finding and mending the kite belongs to the paragraph before it, and the passage never argues that contests are the best way to solve problems. Strategy: match a paragraph to its job, and check that the job is not already done somewhere else.

rc.q: The closing words, “until a bridge stood where a boy's kite string had gone first,” show that the author views Homan's flight as
c: a lucky accident that the engineers did not really need.
a small act that made a much larger structure possible.
an ordinary errand that any child nearby could have run.
a reckless stunt that the author quietly disapproves of.
rc.e: Setting the thin string beside the finished bridge in one sentence is the author's way of honoring a small beginning. The lucky-accident reading fails because the engineers announced the contest precisely to get that first line, and the ordinary-errand reading is contradicted by the wind reasoning and the eight-day wait. Strategy: ask what an author's final image is quietly praising.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Graphite is a soft form of carbon once mistaken for a kind of lead.
Pencils with more clay leave fainter lines than pencils with more graphite.
A pencil is made by baking a mixed core and closing it in grooved boards.
Pencil casings are made from soft cedar rather than a harder wood.
rc.e: The passage moves from the graphite-and-clay paste, through firing and waxing, to the two grooved boards glued around the finished cores, and the closing line names that method outright. A main idea has to cover both the core and the wood, not one recipe detail, not the wood alone, and not the opening fact about the name. Strategy: pick the choice that accounts for the last paragraph as well as the first.

y.A: This is true, but it is only the opening hook, and the passage spends four more paragraphs on how the pencil is actually put together.
y.B: This is a real detail from the third paragraph, but it explains one recipe rather than the whole process the passage traces.
y.D: The cedar is real and the passage does call it soft, but this covers only the wood around the core and leaves out everything the passage says about the core itself.

rc.q: According to the passage, why does a pencil slide instead of scratching?
c: The graphite was stirred with clay and water.
The baked core has been soaked in warm wax.
The wood around it is soft, straight cedar.
The paste was squeezed through a round hole.
rc.e: The sentence about the wax says outright "which is why" a pencil slides instead of scratching, so the cause is stated and does not have to be guessed at. The other choices all borrow real steps and details from the passage, which is exactly what makes them tempting; none of them is offered as the reason for the smooth feel. Strategy: when a sentence contains the words "which is why", the answer to a why question is usually sitting right in front of it.

y.A: That really happens, but the passage ties the clay to binding the powder and to how hard and how dark the line is, not to how smoothly the pencil moves.
y.C: The cedar is real, and it is soft, but the passage brings it up to explain the boards, not the feel of the writing.
y.D: That is how the paste is shaped into a strand, which happens long before the core is finished and says nothing about sliding.

rc.q: Based on the passage, if the grooves in the two boards did not line up when they were glued, the finished pencils would most likely
c: leave a fainter line on the paper.
come out round instead of six-sided.
need a second soak in warm wax.
break as soon as they were sharpened.
rc.e: The passage never mentions grooves that fail to meet, but it does say what goes wrong when a core sits off center: it snaps at the first sharpening. Grooves that do not line up would leave the core off center, so the stated consequence carries straight over. Strategy: when a question describes something the passage never names, look for the nearest thing the passage does warn about and ask whether it would happen here too.

y.A: A fainter line comes from more clay in the core, which is decided back at the mixing stage and has nothing to do with where the groove sits.
y.B: Round and six-sided are both real shapes from the same sentence, but the passage treats that as a choice made when the pencils are shaped, not a result of a crooked groove.
y.C: The wax soak is a real step, and it happens to the cores before they ever reach the boards, so gluing could not send them back for another one.

rc.q: In the fourth paragraph, *wander* most nearly means
c: to drift off a straight line.
to roam with no goal in mind.
to lose track of a thought.
rc.e: The clause right after the word says what the trouble turns out to be: a core sitting off center. So the drill is not roaming about for its own amusement; it is drifting away from the straight path it was started on. The roaming meaning is the one most readers meet first, which is exactly what makes it worth testing inside the sentence and then rejecting. Strategy: read the clause just after the word and ask what problem it names.

y.B: This is the meaning the word usually carries, and it fits a person on a walk, but a drill in a machine has no choice about where it is going.
y.C: A long hole would take time to drill, yet the sentence is worried about where the hole ends up, not about how long it takes.
y.D: A mind can wander in this sense, and the word is genuine, but nothing in the paragraph is thinking about anything.

rc.q: The fourth paragraph raises the idea of drilling a hole mainly in order to
c: show that pencils were once made a different way.
explain why pencils are assembled instead.
list the steps in mixing the gray paste.
caution readers about sharpening too hard.
rc.e: The paragraph names the method a reader would expect, gives two reasons it would fail, and then introduces the real method with the word instead, so the drilling exists to set up the contrast. This is a very common shape in explanations: the wrong idea first, so the right one has something to push against. Strategy: when a paragraph says "You might expect", look for the correction that follows and ask what the setup is doing for it.

y.A: The paragraph offers drilling as something a reader might expect, not as something pencil makers used to do; the passage never mentions an older method at all.
y.C: The mixing steps are all in the second paragraph, and by the fourth paragraph the cores are already finished.
y.D: Sharpening comes up only to show what would go wrong with an off-center core, not as advice about how to sharpen a pencil.

rc.q: The author calls the glued assembly a *sandwich* in order to suggest that
c: the core lies between two layers of wood.
the wood is built up from many thin sheets.
the two boards are pressed together while soft.
the boards are stacked in a pile to dry.
rc.e: A sandwich is a filling held between two slices, which is exactly what the paragraph has just described: cores laid in the grooves of the lower board and the second board pressed on top. Counting extra layers, or reading the word as being about soft wood, misses that the comparison is being made about arrangement. Strategy: ask what two things the image is putting side by side before deciding what it means.

y.B: A sandwich can be piled up in several layers, which makes this tempting, but the paragraph gives the pencil exactly two boards with the cores between them.
y.C: Pressing is in the sentence and the cedar is called soft, yet the comparison is about how the parts are arranged, not about anything bending.
y.D: Drying does happen earlier, to the cores, and the boards in this sentence are glued together rather than stacked and waiting.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Neel is a more patient teacher than Dalia had expected him to be.
Practicing over a bed is what keeps a beginner from giving up.
Dalia turns out to be naturally quick with her hands.
Dalia learns to juggle by fixing the throw instead of the catch.
rc.e: Every step of the story pushes Dalia away from catching and toward the throw: the handing mistake, the Thursday drill in which both bags are allowed to land, and the sentence where the second throw stops being a decision. The choice about the bed picks up a real detail that is far too narrow to be the main idea. Strategy: the main idea has to cover the whole passage, not one true sentence inside it.

y.A: Neel is patient, but the passage never says Dalia expected anything else of him, and how good a teacher he is is not what the story is about.
y.B: The bed is one true detail in one sentence; a single detail is too small to be the point of the whole passage.
y.C: She is not quick at all — she repeats one throw eighty times and drops two bags sixty more, which is the opposite of natural talent.

rc.q: According to the passage, why did Dalia and Neel practice over the bed?
c: so a dropped bag would not thump on the floor below
so a dropped bag did not have to be picked up off the carpet
so the highest throws would have plenty of open room above them
so Dalia would not have to share the room with anyone else
rc.e: The reason is stated in the same sentence that names the bed: bending to pick things off a carpet is how people quit. The bags do thump onto the quilt later, but that thumping is never offered as a reason for choosing the spot. Strategy: when the passage gives a reason in the word because, take that one and stop hunting.

y.A: This sounds like a sensible reason for practicing over a bed, but the passage never mentions the floor below or gives noise as the reason for the spot.
y.C: This sounds sensible for juggling, but the passage says nothing about the height of the room.
y.D: The room is Neel's and no one else appears in it, but the passage gives a different reason outright.

rc.q: What Neel showed Dalia on Thursday felt to her “like being told to fail” most likely because
c: she believed Neel had run out of ways to teach her the skill.
letting the bags land was the thing she had been trying to prevent.
she had thrown well on Tuesday and expected a harder task instead.
she had wanted to move on to all three bags that same afternoon.
rc.e: Up to Thursday, a bag on the quilt was what going wrong looked like, so a drill in which she stands with her hands open and lets both bags land asks her to do the failing on purpose. The passage shows Neel still teaching her afterwards, which rules out the idea that he had nothing left to offer. Strategy: read the sentences just before a feeling to find what caused it.

y.A: Neel keeps teaching her and hands her a third bag two days later, so nothing in the passage suggests he was out of ideas.
y.C: Tuesday did go well, but the passage never shows her wanting something harder — the trouble came as soon as there were two bags.
y.D: She does reach three bags eventually, but the passage never says she was impatient to get there.

rc.q: In the last paragraph, *pattern* most nearly means
c: a design printed on a piece of cloth.
a paper guide for cutting out cloth.
the repeating shape the bags made.
a habit someone repeats without thinking.
rc.e: The pattern hangs in the air for eleven throws and then comes apart, so it is the shape three bags trace as they go up and over again and again. The printed-cloth meaning is the one a reader thinks of first, which is exactly why it is offered here. Strategy: put each dictionary meaning back into the actual sentence and see which one still makes sense.

y.A: That is the meaning most readers meet first, but nothing in this paragraph is printed or made of cloth.
y.B: This is a real meaning of the word, and it belongs to sewing; nobody in the passage is cutting anything out.
y.D: Dalia has certainly built a habit, but this pattern hangs in the air and then comes apart, so it is something visible rather than something inside her.

rc.q: The last paragraph differs from the paragraphs before it mainly because it
c: shows the skill working with no new instruction given.
returns to the bus stop where the passage first began.
saves the hardest of Neel's instructions for the end.
explains the rules a juggler is expected to follow.
rc.e: Each earlier paragraph carries something Neel gives her to do — start with one, forty times and then forty more, that is handing, and the drill he throws for her on Thursday. The last one says plainly that there was nothing new to tell, and spends its space on eleven throws that work. Strategy: ask what a paragraph does differently from the ones around it, not only what it mentions.

y.B: Stories often circle back to where they opened, but this one stays in Neel's room; the bus stop is never mentioned again.
y.C: The passage says the opposite — Neel tells her nothing new on Saturday.
y.D: The paragraph shows one girl juggling; it does not set out rules for juggling in general.

rc.q: The comparison “like someone passing a note” suggests that Dalia was
c: moving the bag across rather than throwing it up.
handling the bag as gently as a folded piece of paper.
trying to hide what she was doing from her cousin.
growing tired after tossing one bag eighty times.
rc.e: A note travels from one hand to another; nobody throws one across a room. That is exactly what Dalia does with the second beanbag, and the next sentence puts a name to it: handing, not throwing. Strategy: ask what the two things being compared actually have in common before you choose.

y.B: A note is a delicate thing, so gentleness is the first idea the comparison brings to mind, but the comparison is about the path the bag takes, not about how softly she holds it.
y.C: Notes are often passed secretly, and that association is what makes this tempting; Neel is watching her closely and she is hiding nothing.
y.D: She really does throw one bag eighty times, but a true detail from the paragraph before does not explain what this comparison means.

rc.q: The passage is mainly about
c: a grandmother who teaches her granddaughter to swim across a lake.
a girl who gets thoroughly soaked during an early morning on a lake.
a girl who becomes strong enough to row after an hour of hard practice.
a girl who discovers that skill, not raw force, is what moves a boat.
rc.e: The last lines say plainly that Nadia “was not stronger than she had been an hour before” but “had simply stopped fighting the thing she was trying to move.” The choice about growing strong enough is tempting because it is what usually happens in practice stories, but the passage denies it in so many words. Strategy: when a story ends by correcting an expectation, that correction is the main idea.

rc.q: What happens the first time Nadia pulls with all her weight?
c: The boat slides forward without a sound and the ripples spread behind in even rings.
The blades slap the surface, spray soaks her knees, and the boat barely moves.
The heron on the shore is startled by the noise and flies off quickly.
One of the wooden oars snaps in half and drops into the cold water.
rc.e: The second paragraph states that the boat barely moved, the blades slapped the surface, and the spray soaked her knees. The silent forward glide describes the later, corrected stroke, and the startled heron reverses the bird, which watches her and then lifts away “without hurrying.” Strategy: check that a detail belongs to the part of the story the question asks about.

rc.q: The grandmother most likely says nothing at first because she
c: is annoyed with her granddaughter and has decided not to speak to her again.
does not know how to row a boat and so has nothing useful to offer.
has quietly fallen asleep in the stern of the boat while Nadia works.
wants Nadia to feel the problem herself before she is told how to fix it.
rc.e: Her silence is called “her way of teaching,” and she speaks only after Nadia's hard pulling has failed, giving three exact instructions. The choice about not knowing how to row is impossible given how expert that advice turns out to be, and her folded hands and watchful stillness rule out sleep. Strategy: when a story labels a behavior, use that label to explain the character's purpose.

rc.q: When the grandmother says, “Let it bite,” she means that the blade should
c: drop all the way to the lake bottom.
sting the hands sharply and painfully.
take firm hold of the water.
cut into something with sharp teeth.
rc.e: The next paragraph shows exactly what she meant: Nadia lowers the blade and feels “the water take hold of it, a firm and surprising grip.” Cutting with teeth is the everyday meaning of the word and has nothing to do with an oar. Strategy: when a word is used oddly, read on — a story often shows you the meaning a sentence later.

rc.q: The paragraph that begins with the grandmother's instruction is the turning point of the passage because it
c: replaces Nadia's effort with a method, and the boat's behavior changes at once.
returns to the heron on the shore in order to slow the whole story down.
explains why the lake lies so calm and still early on a summer morning.
introduces a new character who takes over the rowing from Nadia herself.
rc.e: Before it, the boat barely moves and the handles jump from her grip; right after the instruction, the boat “slid forward without a sound” and the ripples spread in even rings. The choice about a new character is false, since the grandmother never rows. Strategy: to find a turning point, compare what is true just before it with what is true just after.

rc.q: The phrase “the oars quarreled with the water, arguing over every stroke” suggests that
c: the oars were old and creaked loudly in their worn metal locks.
the lake was rough and choppy that morning and full of waves.
Nadia was muttering complaints to herself the whole time she rowed.
Nadia's strokes and the water were working against each other.
rc.e: Giving the oars a quarrel is a way of picturing effort that fights the water instead of using it, which is why the boat barely moves. The rough-lake choice is contradicted by the opening description of a lake “perfectly still.” Strategy: ask what the figure of speech is describing in plain terms before choosing.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Road salt is the only substance that is able to clear ice from a winter road surface.
Sand is spread on the roads in very cold places because it helps tires grip the icy surface.
Winter storms across the country have become far more dangerous over the last thirty years.
Salt keeps water from freezing on roads, but within limits and at a cost, so crews now use less.
rc.e: The passage explains how salt works, states the temperature limit, describes the harm meltwater carries into soil and streams, and ends with brine spraying that “uses far less salt.” The sand choice is one detail from the second paragraph, and the claim that salt is the only ice remover is contradicted by the sand crews use in the coldest places. Strategy: a main idea has to cover the turn as well as the opening.

rc.q: According to the passage, why do trucks spread salt before the snow begins to fall?
c: Because salt melts ice much faster while the pavement is still dry and clear.
To keep a thin film of water from freezing onto the pavement in the first place.
Because the trucks cannot drive safely on a road once the snow has covered it over.
Because salt loses all of its melting power once the crystals become wet.
rc.e: The first paragraph says the salt “is not there only to melt ice that has already formed” but to stop a film of water from freezing onto the pavement to begin with. The choice about salt losing its power when wet is contradicted by the last paragraph, where crews deliberately dissolve salt into brine before spraying it. Strategy: read the sentence that follows a “not only” — it usually carries the real answer.

rc.q: Based on the passage, in which situation would a crew be most likely to choose sand instead of salt?
c: A week when the crew's main goal is to lower the freezing point of water on the pavement.
A wet afternoon in early spring when the temperature stays near fifty degrees.
A night when the temperature is expected to fall to twenty below zero.
A storm arriving at thirty degrees, when the crew wants to stop ice from forming at all.
rc.e: Salted water stays liquid only down to about six degrees below zero; colder than that the salt is “simply cold grit,” which is why the coldest places use sand. The choice about lowering the freezing point is ruled out by the flat statement that “sand cannot lower a freezing point at all.” Strategy: apply the limit the passage gives to the numbers in each choice.

rc.q: As used in the first paragraph, “solution” most nearly means
c: a liquid with something dissolved in it.
a hard crust of salt and ice on the road.
an answer to a difficult problem or puzzle.
a plan that a city government agrees to follow.
rc.e: The sentence describes what forms when salt particles dissolve in water and then stay liquid below freezing, so the word names the salty liquid itself. The answer-to-a-problem sense is the word's everyday meaning and is especially tempting because the passage is about solving a winter problem. Strategy: prefer the scientific sense when the sentence is describing what a substance is, not what someone decided.

rc.q: What is the purpose of the short sentence “There is a limit.”?
c: It explains why many crews now spray brine on the pavement before a storm.
It simply repeats the main point of the first paragraph in fewer words.
It marks a turn from how salt works to the conditions in which it stops working.
It introduces the harm that meltwater does to roadside trees and to streams.
rc.e: Everything before it explains why salted water stays liquid; everything after it gives the freezing point, the minus-six limit, and the switch to sand. The meltwater harm and the brine spraying are real parts of the passage, but they come later, in the third and fourth paragraphs. Strategy: a short sentence set on its own is usually a hinge — read what changes right after it.

rc.q: The closing sentences — “The chemistry has not changed. What has changed is how carefully it is spent.” — suggest that the author sees the switch to brine as
c: a change in everyday practice, not a new scientific discovery.
a sign that scientists no longer agree about how water freezes.
proof that road salt has stopped working the way it once did.
a warning that brine harms the streams more than dry salt does.
rc.e: The pair of sentences separates the science, which is unchanged, from the habit of using less of it, which is what crews have altered. The choice calling brine more harmful is contradicted by the same paragraph, which says brine “uses far less salt.” Strategy: when an author sets two short sentences against each other, the second one carries the point.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: The Moon does not spin at all, which is why one face always points at us.
The Moon's far side was first photographed by a spacecraft that flew behind it.
The half we never see is permanently dark, unlike the half that faces Earth.
Earth's pull settled the Moon into a spin that matches its orbit.
rc.e: The passage sets up a puzzle in the first paragraph (the Moon must turn once per lap to keep one face toward us) and spends the third paragraph explaining what put it into that rhythm. The choice about the 1959 spacecraft is true but is a single closing detail, and the choice about a permanently dark half is contradicted in the last paragraph. Strategy: the main idea has to cover the whole passage, not one sentence of it.

y.A: This is the exact guess the first paragraph calls the reverse of the truth, so it is the idea the passage sets out to correct.
y.B: That happens in the very last sentence, and one closing fact is far too small to be what the whole passage is about.
y.C: The passage says outright that the hidden half gets as much sunlight as the half we know.

rc.q: According to the passage, what is happening on the far side of the Moon when the Moon looks full to us?
c: It is dark there for all time.
It is going through its night.
It is turned toward the Sun.
It is warmer than the near side.
rc.e: The last paragraph states it directly: when the Moon looks full to us, the far side is in night. The choice about lasting darkness borrows the name people use for that half, which is the very name the paragraph calls wrong. Strategy: for a detail question, find the sentence that mentions the thing the question names, and read it all the way to the end.

y.A: This is the dark-side idea the paragraph is written to correct, since the far side gets as much sunlight as the half we know.
y.C: A full Moon means our side is the lit one, so the far side is the side facing away from the sunlight just then.
y.D: The passage never compares the two halves for warmth. It says only which one is in night.

rc.q: The passage suggests that if the Moon's orbit were a perfect circle,
c: the Moon would stop turning on its axis.
the far side would get sunlight of its own.
observers would have less of the Moon to chart.
the Moon would need much longer to finish a lap.
rc.e: The thin strip of the far side that observers managed to chart comes from the rocking, and the rocking comes from the Moon hurrying and lagging in an orbit that is not a true circle. Take the uneven orbit away and that strip goes with it, so there would be less of the Moon to map than the little-more-than-half they reached. Strategy: when a question removes a cause, follow the chain the passage already built and ask which effect shrinks.

y.A: Nothing in the passage ties the shape of the orbit to whether the Moon turns. The spin was settled long ago by the bulge.
y.B: The far side already gets as much sunlight as the near side, so a rounder orbit would change nothing about that.
y.D: The passage says the orbit's shape makes the Moon hurry and lag along the way, not that it changes how long a lap takes.

rc.q: In the third paragraph, *faint* most nearly means
c: so slight it is hard to notice.
weak and about to fall over.
too quiet to be heard clearly.
rc.e: The bulge is the small stretch that Earth's slightly stronger pull produces, so faint here means barely there, hardly noticeable. The dizzy and the quiet-sound meanings are both genuine senses of the word, which is what makes them tempting, but neither fits a shape in rock. Strategy: read each meaning back into the actual sentence and keep the one that still makes sense.

y.B: That is a real meaning of the word, but rock does not feel dizzy, and the sentence is describing a shape.
y.C: A bulge is something you could see or measure, not something that makes a sound.
y.D: This meaning turns up in words like faint-hearted, and nothing in a stretched piece of rock is being called cowardly.

rc.q: The second paragraph mainly serves to
c: let the reader act out the Moon's once-per-lap turn.
introduce the gravity explained in the paragraph after it.
prove that a chair and a moon obey the same laws.
show that the Moon's motion is too odd to picture.
rc.e: The first paragraph makes a claim that sounds wrong at first hearing, and the chair paragraph hands the reader a way to perform that same turn and feel that it is true. It introduces no new cause and it argues nothing about laws. Strategy: ask what a short paragraph does for the paragraph before it, not just what objects it mentions.

y.B: Gravity does not appear anywhere in the chair paragraph; it arrives fresh at the start of the next one.
y.C: The paragraph asks the reader to walk one circle, and nothing more. It never claims that a chair and a moon are governed by the same laws, which would be a far larger claim than this passage makes anywhere.
y.D: The paragraph does the opposite, making the motion easy to picture by putting the reader inside it.

rc.q: In saying that the same dark patches *stare back*, the author suggests that
c: the Moon is keeping watch over Earth.
the same view meets us each time.
the dark patches slowly change shape.
the patches are hard to see clearly.
rc.e: Patches of rock cannot stare, so the phrase has to mean something else, and the two words before it say what: tonight, and again next month, the same ones. It is a way of saying the view never changes. Strategy: when a writer gives an object a human action, ask what the action is standing in for, and look at the words around it for the answer.

y.A: This takes the staring literally. The patches are markings, and the author is describing what we see, not something the Moon is doing on purpose.
y.C: The whole point of the sentence is that the patches do not change, which is what makes the rest of the passage surprising.
y.D: The patches are the part that is easy to see; the passage never says anything about how hard they are to make out.

rc.q: The author's main purpose in this passage is to
c: explain why the grade of Hill Street is gentler at the park gate than at the top.
argue that Hill Street needs benches back and that the town must keep them up.
describe how one neighbor has done her shopping on foot for the past fifty years.
persuade neighbors to take turns driving Ruth up the hill to the grocery store.
rc.e: The first paragraph makes the request — benches back on Hill Street, spaced so that nobody climbs a whole block without a stop — and the third paragraph adds the other half of it, that the washing and the painting come out of the same budget as the benches. Everything else supports that request: the slope sets it up, Ruth shows what a bench does, the ending says what is at stake. Strategy: the main idea has to account for the whole argument, including the part about upkeep.

y.A: The slope is described in the opening lines, but it is the setting for the argument rather than the thing the author is asking the town to do.
y.C: Ruth is one example used to support the request, and a main idea has to cover the whole passage, not a single person inside it.
y.D: The car does appear in the passage, but the author is addressing the town and asking for benches, not organizing rides for anybody.

rc.q: According to the passage, what did Ruth do while the bench outside the bakery was still there?
c: She had her groceries brought to her by car on Tuesdays.
She walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down.
She waited at the bench for someone to drive her up the hill.
She carried her shopping up the hill and walked back down.
rc.e: One sentence in the second paragraph answers this directly: while the bench stood outside the bakery, she walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down. The sentence after it describes the present arrangement, groceries arriving by car, and one choice turns her trip around so that the shopping goes uphill. Strategy: when a passage describes a before and an after, put your finger on which one the question asks about, then check the direction of travel.

y.A: That is what happens now that the bench is gone, so this choice puts the after-picture into the before-slot.
y.C: Nobody in the passage waits at the bench for a ride; the bench is a place to stop partway through her own climb.
y.D: Every piece of this is in the sentence, but the trip runs the other way: she walked up and carried the shopping down.

rc.q: Suppose the town offered to install twelve benches but would not pay to wash or repaint them. Based on the passage, the author would most likely
c: prefer six benches the town has promised to look after.
accept the twelve, since more places to stop is the goal.
ask that the money go toward widening the sidewalk instead.
agree, if neighbors themselves did the washing and painting.
rc.e: The author has already faced this exact trade. There is room on Hill Street for twelve, and the author asks for six anyway, on the grounds that benches nobody looks after splinter before long — so a smaller number with the upkeep attached is the deal the author chose once cost was the objection. Strategy: when a question invents a new situation, look for the place where the author has already made the same choice.

y.B: More benches sounds like more of what the author wants, but the author says plainly that the ask is six with upkeep, even though twelve would fit on the street.
y.C: A wider sidewalk was the town's own answer last time, and the second paragraph exists to say that a bench does what widening cannot.
y.D: The author asks for the upkeep to come out of the town's budget, and nowhere offers to take that work on.

rc.q: In the first paragraph, *grade* most nearly means
c: a mark given on a piece of schoolwork.
a level of school, such as fifth year.
the quality or rank of a material.
the slope of a rising road.
rc.e: The sentence sets the word between gentle and steep and attaches it to a street that earns the name Hill, so it has to mean the slope itself — how sharply the road rises. The two school meanings are real meanings of the word, which is exactly why they are offered here. Strategy: read the whole sentence with each meaning slotted in and keep the one that still makes sense.

y.A: This is the meaning you meet most often at school, but a park gate cannot be given a mark.
y.B: A street does not have school years, and the sentence is comparing the bottom of the hill with the top.
y.C: The word can describe how good a material is, but here gentle and steep are describing a slope, not a quality.

rc.q: The last two sentences of the passage mainly serve to
c: restate the cost of upkeep that the third paragraph accepts.
recall how Ruth used the bench outside the bakery.
admit what benches cannot do and name what they decide.
predict how many people will sit on the benches each week.
rc.e: Having said what a bench does, the author closes by giving one thing up and claiming another: the hill will stay exactly as steep as it was, and the benches will settle who is able to walk up it. Neither sentence goes back to the money, and neither counts anybody. Strategy: a closing line often concedes something small in order to hold on to something large — read the ending for that trade.

y.A: The cost of keeping benches up is granted in the paragraph before this one, and the closing lines never return to it.
y.B: Ruth's Tuesdays belong to the second paragraph, and the ending does not go back to her.
y.D: The author never counts users; the last line is about who is able to climb the hill, not how many will sit down.

rc.q: In the last paragraph the author calls a sidewalk with benches “a room” in order to suggest that
c: benches turn a place people pass through into a place they stay.
benches take up as much space as the walls of a small building.
the town should build a shelter over the sidewalk on Hill Street.
a bench can make a public sidewalk feel like part of a home.
rc.e: A corridor is somewhere you walk through on your way elsewhere, and the author sets it against a room, then says straight out that people stay in rooms and offers two small pictures of staying. The figure is about what the sidewalk becomes for the people on it, not about the size of a bench or about turning a public place into a private one. Strategy: when an author makes a comparison, read the sentence just after it, which usually tells you what the comparison is for.

y.B: The passage does compare a bench to a small building, but that comparison is about upkeep, not about how much room a bench fills.
y.C: Nobody is asking for a roof here; the room is a way of describing the sidewalk, not a thing to be built on top of it.
y.D: A room does suggest a house, but the contrast the author draws is corridor against room — passing through against staying — not public against private.

RC-SEP-W1-S1-P.x: A vacant city lot had collected litter for years. When neighbors proposed a community garden, some residents doubted that vegetables could grow beside tall buildings.
