VR.e: Reluctant means hesitant or unwilling; being unable is different from not wanting to act.

VR.q: SPARSE most nearly means:
VR.e: Sparse means thinly scattered or not dense; texture, flatness, and color do not express low density.

VR.q: VERIFY most nearly means:
VR.e: To verify is to confirm that something is true or accurate; arranging, announcing, or merely comparing does not establish truth.

VR.q: The gardener spread straw around the young plants to ____ the soil from drying too quickly.
VR.e: Straw can prevent rapid drying by slowing evaporation; loosening, measuring, and decorating do not fit the stated purpose.

VR.q: Although the directions seemed ____, following them produced a complicated paper sculpture.
VR.e: Although signals contrast between simple directions and a complicated result; the other choices do not create that clear contrast.

VR.q: The creek was unusually ____ after the storm, so the hikers used the bridge instead of stepping across.
VR.e: Storm water can make a creek swollen and unsafe to step across; clear, shallow, or calm water would not explain using the bridge.

VR.q: Because the two accounts ____ each other, the reporter checked which one was accurate.
VR.e: Accounts that contradict each other cannot both be accurate in the same way, so checking is logical; entertaining, copying, or completing one another would not create the stated uncertainty.

VR.q: The watchmaker needed a ____ tool that could lift a gear no wider than a grain of rice.
VR.e: A tiny gear requires a delicate, precise tool; weight, familiarity, and price do not show suitability for fine work.

VR.q: Nia listened to both sides of the disagreement before deciding, showing that she was ____.
VR.e: Hearing both sides before judging demonstrates fairness; inventiveness and timidity are irrelevant, and impatience conflicts with listening.

VR.q: Before planting the seeds, Raul ____ the rows with small wooden stakes.
VR.e: Marking rows logically happens before planting; harvesting comes later, while watering or erasing does not establish locations.

VR.q: The principal's reminder was ____ rather than accusing; it focused on the rule, not on blaming anyone.
VR.e: A neutral reminder avoids accusation and blame; impatience, humor, and indirectness are not established by the clues.

VR.q: The old diary was ____, with several pages missing and others too faded to read.
VR.e: Missing and unreadable pages make the record incomplete; value, privacy, and binding do not address lost content.

VR.q: When clouds covered the sun, the temperature began to ____.
VR.e: Less direct sunlight can cause temperature to drop; the other verbs do not sensibly describe temperature in this context.

VR.q: The committee invited a soil expert to ____ whether the vacant lot could support a garden.
VR.e: An expert can assess, or evaluate, the soil's suitability; celebrating, promising, and remembering do not answer the question.

VR.q: The scratch was so ____ that it disappeared after one light coat of polish.
VR.e: Easy removal with one light coat shows the scratch was minor; its shape, age, or shine does not explain the result.

VR.q: The twins look nearly identical, but their interests are quite ____.
VR.e: But contrasts similar appearance with distinct, or different, interests; the other adjectives do not establish difference.

VR.q: The ____ cook turned yesterday's rice and a few leftover vegetables into a delicious soup.
VR.e: Turning leftovers into a good meal shows a resourceful cook; gentle, forgetful, and athletic do not explain making much from little.

VR.q: The new schedule will ____ effect on Monday, when the buses begin arriving earlier.
VR.e: “Take effect” is the correct idiom for beginning to operate; the other verbs do not form the standard expression.

VR.q: Compared with the rough first draft, the final poster looked ____.
VR.e: Revision makes a final product polished; the other choices do not logically contrast with a rough draft.

VR.q: The historian included two letters from the period to ____ her claim about daily life.
VR.e: Period letters provide evidence that can support a historical claim; postponing, shortening, or disguising does not use evidence logically.

QR.q: A scooter travels 42 miles on 3 gallons of fuel. A small cart travels 65 miles on 5 gallons. How many more miles per gallon does the scooter travel?
QR.e: The rates are 14 and 13 miles per gallon, so the scooter travels 1 more; C and D are individual rates, while A subtracts the gallons rather than the rates.

QR.q: A mural crew paints 2/7 of a wall Monday and 3/14 Tuesday. What fraction of the wall remains unpainted?
QR.e: Painted = 4/14 + 3/14 = 7/14, leaving 7/14 = 1/2; the other fractions come from subtracting or stopping too early.

QR.q: A theater adds seats to four rehearsal rows in this pattern: 11, 15, 22, 32. If the increases grow by 3 each time, how many seats are in the next row?
QR.e: The increases are 4, 7, and 10, so the next is 13; 32 + 13 = 45. The other choices use a wrong next increase.

QR.q: A trail mix uses raisins and seeds in a ratio of 5:4. A 72-ounce batch contains how many ounces of seeds?
QR.e: Nine parts equal 72, so each part is 8; seeds are 4 × 8 = 32. B halves the total, D uses the raisin parts, and A mis-scales.

QR.q: A library shelf is 60% full when it holds 48 books. How many books fit when the shelf is completely full?
QR.e: If 48 is 60%, the whole is 48 ÷ 0.60 = 80; the distractors add a percentage or use an incorrect scale.

QR.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 4 blue, 3 green, 2 yellow, and 1 red. What is the probability of not landing on blue?
QR.e: Six of ten sections are not blue, and 6/10 = 3/5; A is the blue probability, while C and D miscount nonblue sections.

QR.q: A club pays a $6 setup fee plus $4 per badge. Its bill is $38. How many badges did it order?
QR.e: Subtract the $6 fee to get $32, then divide by $4 for 8 badges; A and B mishandle the fee, and D adds instead of undoing.

QR.q: Four water samples have an average volume of 26 milliliters. Three contain 21, 24, and 28 milliliters. What is the fourth volume?
QR.e: The total is 4 × 26 = 104; known volumes total 73, leaving 31. The others result from averaging only known values or subtracting incorrectly.

QR.q: A warehouse packs 4,116 pencils equally into 79 cartons. About how many pencils go in each carton?
QR.e: Use 4,000 ÷ 80 = 50; 500 is a place-value error, and 40 or 60 are poorer estimates.

QR.q: A map marker at (−4, 2) moves 7 units east and 5 units north. What are its new coordinates?
QR.e: East adds 7 to x and north adds 5 to y, giving (3, 7); the distractors reverse signs, directions, or coordinate changes.

QR.q: A rectangular pen has a perimeter of 46 meters and a width of 8 meters. What is its length?
QR.e: 2(L + 8) = 46, so L + 8 = 23 and L = 15; A subtracts width twice, B subtracts width from the full perimeter, and C confuses length with a two-side total.

QR.q: Mei presents before Luis. Luis presents before Tori. Which statement must be true?
QR.e: The chain Mei–Luis–Tori guarantees Mei is before Tori; the other choices reverse or contradict the order.

QR.q: Four recipes use 5/12, 7/16, 9/20, and 11/24 cup of oil. Which amount is greatest?
QR.e: The values are about .417, .438, .450, and .458; 11/24 is greatest. The distractors reflect numerator-only or denominator-only comparison.

QR.q: On a trail map, 2.5 centimeters represent 10 kilometers. How far does 7 centimeters represent?
QR.e: The scale is 4 km per cm, so 7 cm represents 28 km; B multiplies by 2.5, while C and D use incorrect scales.

QR.q: A box holds 4 silver, 7 gold, and 9 copper coins. One coin is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is silver or gold?
QR.e: There are 4 + 7 + 9 = 20 coins, and 4 + 7 = 11 of them are silver or gold, so the probability is 11/20. A uses only the silver coins (4/20 = 1/5), B uses only the gold coins, and C gives the probability of copper—the very coins the draw must avoid.

QR.q: A museum tour offers 3 start times and 4 route choices at each time. How many time-and-route combinations are possible?
QR.e: Each of 3 times pairs with 4 routes, so 3 × 4 = 12; A adds categories, while C and D overcount.

QR.q: A pump fills 18 liters every 4 minutes at a steady rate. How many liters does it fill in 14 minutes?
QR.e: The rate is 4.5 liters per minute; 4.5 × 14 = 63. The distractors scale only by whole 4-minute blocks or round the rate.

QR.q: Two display lights flash every 8 seconds and every 12 seconds. If they flash together now, after how many seconds will they next flash together?
QR.e: The least common multiple of 8 and 12 is 24; A adds intervals, while B and D use larger common multiples rather than the next one.

QR.q: After donating 3/8 of a collection, Sam has 45 cards left. How many cards were in the collection at first?
QR.e: The 45 cards are 5/8 of the original, so 45 × 8/5 = 72; the others treat 45 as the donated part or add incorrectly.

QR.q: The lap times are 31, 34, 36, 39, and 44 seconds. A sixth time of 50 seconds is added. What is the new median?
QR.e: With six values, average the third and fourth: (36 + 39)/2 = 37.5; A and C keep a middle value, and D averages the wrong pair.

QR.q: A rectangular banner is 6 feet by 10 feet. Its length is doubled while its width stays the same. How does its area change?
c: It becomes four times as large.
QR.e: Original area is 60 and new area is 120 square feet, so it doubles; fourfold growth would require doubling both dimensions.

QR.q: At dawn the temperature was −6°C. By noon it had risen 11 degrees. What was the noon temperature?
QR.e: −6 + 11 = 5; B subtracts instead, C changes only the sign, and D ignores the starting value.

QR.q: In a group of 32 students, 18 play an instrument, 15 sing, and 7 do both. How many do neither?
QR.e: At least one activity = 18 + 15 − 7 = 26, so neither = 32 − 26 = 6. A follows an addition slip in totaling 18 + 15 (35 − 7 = 28, then 32 − 28 = 4), B repeats the 7 who do both, and D counts the instrument-only students (18 − 7 = 11) instead of those doing neither.

QR.q: Every zep is a lum. No lum is square. Which statement must be true?
QR.e: Since all zeps are lums and no lum is square, no zep can be square; the other choices reverse the relation or assume existence.

QR.q: A $80 backpack is discounted 25%, then a $6 coupon is applied. What is the final price?
QR.e: A 25% discount removes $20, leaving $60; subtracting $6 gives $54. The distractors omit or misorder a reduction.

QR.q: A rental cost is described by 3(2h + 5) − 4. Which expression gives the same cost?
QR.e: Distribute to get 6h + 15, then subtract 4 for 6h + 11; the others fail to distribute or combine constants correctly.

QR.q: A closed cube-shaped gift box has edges 4 inches long. How many square inches of paper cover its six faces exactly?
QR.e: Each face is 4 × 4 = 16 square inches; six faces total 96. A uses edge totals, C is volume, and D miscounts faces.

QR.q: A game score follows 4, 12, 15, 45, 48, ... by alternating two operations. What is the next score?
QR.e: The rule alternates ×3, +3; after 48, multiply by 3 to get 144. A repeats +3, and B or D use wrong multipliers.

QR.q: A chef has 3 1/2 liters of soup and fills containers holding 1/4 liter each. How many full containers can be filled?
QR.e: 3 1/2 = 14/4, so fourteen 1/4-liter containers can be filled; the distractors multiply or use only the whole-number part.

QR.q: A teacher arranges 286 tiles in rows of 9. How many tiles are left after making as many complete rows as possible?
QR.e: 9 × 31 = 279, leaving 286 − 279 = 7; the other remainders come from nearby multiples or digit shortcuts.

QR.q: Team Red's times are 12, 15, 15, 18, 20. Team Blue's are 10, 14, 16, 19, 22. How much greater is Team Blue's range?
QR.e: Red's range is 8 and Blue's is 12, a difference of 4; A compares minima, B gives Red's range, and D gives Blue's range.

QR.q: A straight path and a diagonal path meet, forming adjacent angles. One angle is 68°. What is the other angle?
QR.e: Adjacent angles on a straight line total 180°, so 180 − 68 = 112°; A uses 90°, B assumes equality, and C subtracts incorrectly.

QR.q: The first box holds 30 books on 5 shelves. The second box holds 42 books on 7 shelves. Which statement is true?
c: The first box holds more per shelf.
They hold the same number per shelf.
The second box holds 2 more per shelf.
The second box holds 12 more per shelf.
QR.e: Both rates equal 6 books per shelf (30 ÷ 5 = 6 and 42 ÷ 7 = 6). A assumes fewer shelves means more on each shelf, C reports the difference in shelf counts (7 − 5 = 2) as a per-shelf difference, and D does the same with the totals (42 − 30 = 12).

QR.q: A reservoir rises from 120 centimeters to 150 centimeters. What is the percent increase?
QR.e: The increase is 30, and 30/120 = 25%; B divides by the new amount, C reports the increase as a percent, and D reverses the ratio.

QR.q: A square rug has an area of 190 square feet. Its side length, in feet, is between which pair of consecutive whole numbers?
QR.e: 13 × 13 = 169 and 14 × 14 = 196, and 169 < 190 < 196, so the side is between 13 and 14. A halves 190 instead (9² = 81 and 10² = 100 surround 95), B stops after seeing 12² = 144 fall below 190, and C treats 14 as the lower bound once 14² passes 190.

QR.q: A cyclist travels 18 miles per hour for 1 hour 40 minutes. How far does the cyclist travel?
QR.e: 1 hour 40 minutes = 5/3 hours; 18 × 5/3 = 30. A treats 40 minutes as 1/3 hour, while B and D misconvert time.

QR.q: A badge can use one of 5 shapes and one of 3 colors, but the star shape cannot be green. How many allowed badges are possible?
QR.e: Normally 5 × 3 = 15 combinations; removing the one forbidden star-green pair leaves 14. The others remove too many or none.

QR.q: A rectangular courtyard is 18 meters by 12 meters. A walker completes 3 laps around it. How far does the walker travel?
QR.e: One lap is 2(18 + 12) = 60 meters; three laps total 180. A misses a side, C uses area, and D gives one lap.

RC.q: Which statement best explains what the students learned from the moth survey?
c: Pond insects are always harder to photograph than meadow moths.
Students should collect wildlife data in daylight, not at night.
The brightest lamp is the most reliable way to count moths.
Discovering an unfair condition helped students improve a survey.
RC.e: D captures the problem, revision, and lesson in [¶2–¶4]. A overgeneralizes one detail, B contradicts the successful night survey, and C repeats the condition that made the first comparison unfair.

RC.q: Why were the students unable to compare the first station counts fairly?
c: Some teams forgot their notebooks and lost their counts.
The teams used lamps of different brightness.
The moths were released before anyone recorded the time.
The pond station began counting an hour after the others.
RC.e: [¶2] explicitly says Lena's brighter lamp could attract moths from farther away. A and D are never stated, and C contradicts [¶1], where the students recorded the time before releasing each moth.

RC.q: What can be inferred about the identical lights used in the second count?
c: They made location, rather than brightness, the meaningful difference.
They guaranteed that every moth in the whole meadow was seen and counted.
They caused every station to attract exactly the same kinds of moths.
They made it unnecessary to photograph any of the visiting moths.
RC.e: Controlling brightness lets location be compared more fairly, as [¶3–¶4] imply. B and C claim guarantees the passage does not support, and D is contradicted by the survey method.

RC.q: In [¶3], “settled” most nearly means:
RC.e: The moths became visible when they landed on the sheet. A, B, and D are other meanings of settled that do not fit the physical context.

RC.q: Which sequence best describes the development of the passage?
c: A list of moth species is followed by a description of each kind.
An investigation is described, a flaw noticed, the method improved.
Two students argue about the count until a teacher settles it.
A meadow and a pond are compared in each of the four seasons.
RC.e: [¶1] begins the investigation, [¶2] identifies the flaw, and [¶3–¶4] describe the revision and lesson. The other structures are not present.

RC.q: Which choice best summarizes the discovery beneath Bellweather's steps?
c: Why nineteenth-century buildings often had weak stone foundations
How surveyors searched for buried treasure beneath old town halls
How a town identified and preserved an old survey marker
Why Bellweather replaced its town hall with a history museum
RC.e: C reflects the identification in [¶1–¶2] and preservation in [¶3–¶4]. A is unsupported, B is denied by [¶4], which says the stone revealed no buried treasure, and D never occurs.

RC.q: According to [¶2], why did surveyors place durable markers?
c: To give later mapmakers fixed starting points
To mark where public buildings should be constructed
To decorate the open spaces around the town
To warn people about tunnels running under the town
RC.e: [¶2] directly states that later mapmakers could begin from fixed points. B and D are not given purposes—and [¶4] denies any tunnel—while C repeats the residents' mistaken assumption in [¶1].

RC.q: Why would moving the stone reduce its value as a survey record?
c: Its carved 1882 date would become harder to read.
The new glass panel would no longer fit the landing.
The town hall would lose its front entrance and steps.
Its exact position was the information it preserved.
RC.e: [¶2–¶3] show that the marker's carefully measured location made it useful; moving it would destroy that evidence. A, B, and C concern appearance or construction, not surveying.

RC.q: In [¶4], “quieter” suggests that the stone's importance was:
c: secret from all of the town's residents
related to the silence of the building
less useful than the workers believed
RC.e: [¶4] contrasts the marker with treasure and tunnels, so “quieter” means less dramatic but still meaningful. A, C, and D read the word too literally or reverse the passage's judgment.

RC.q: The author's attitude toward the town's solution is best described as:
RC.e: [¶3–¶4] presents the glass panel as preserving both practical and historical value. A and C conflict with that praise, while B is not supported by humor.

RC.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
c: A brief conversation helps Mara see her nervousness and begin preparing.
Mara decides that drawing pictures is easier than writing stories.
A long train delay keeps Mara from reaching the festival on time.
A stranger on the train persuades Mara to give away her story.
RC.e: [¶2–¶4] shows the sketcher's comment helping Mara shift from avoidance to rehearsal. B, C, and D do not happen.

RC.q: Which action most clearly shows Mara avoiding practice at the beginning?
c: She chose a window seat before the train left.
She watched the sketcher's pencil move quickly.
She reorganized her pencils instead of reading.
She kept her story inside an envelope in her pocket.
RC.e: [¶1] lists pencil organizing among distractions from the view and story. A, B, and D may occur while nervous but do not as clearly replace practice.

RC.q: What does Mara learn from watching the scenery in [¶4]?
c: The festival town is surrounded mostly by open farmland.
Separate moments can still form a complete experience.
Train travel moves too fast for careful observation.
Reading aloud is easier outdoors than on a train.
RC.e: The changing views “held together,” paralleling how selected moments can make a drawing or story. A is incidental, and C and D are unsupported.

RC.q: In [¶2], “escape” suggests that Mara was holding the envelope:
RC.e: If the envelope looked as though it might escape, Mara must have been gripping it tightly. A and B are opposite, while C concerns visibility rather than grip.

RC.q: The mood at the end of the passage is best described as:
RC.e: Mara practices, reaches the town, and stops shaking in [¶4], showing calm improvement rather than gloom, mystery, or extreme excitement.

RC.q: Which statement best summarizes Suri's solution and its result?
c: Outdoor courts are better than halls for every dance rehearsal.
A chalk diagram helped a choreographer plan movement before rehearsal.
Rain forced the dance group to cancel its Saturday performance.
The dancers invented a new game using colored chalk arrows.
RC.e: B covers Suri's planning method and result in [¶1–¶4]. A overstates the method, and C and D contradict the events.

RC.q: Which question could the chalk plan NOT answer?
c: Where should each dancer begin the piece?
Do two paths cross on the same count?
Which routes show dancers moving backward?
Does a lift feel safe to the dancers?
RC.e: [¶4] explicitly says the drawing could not show whether a lift felt safe. A–C are exactly the spatial facts represented by circles, intersecting arrows, and dotted lines.

RC.q: Why was saving hall time especially important?
c: The hall was available only once a week.
The box of sidewalk chalk was expensive.
The dancers disliked rehearsing in the hall.
The final performance had already taken place.
RC.e: [¶1] says the hall was available only on Saturdays, so solving spatial problems beforehand protected limited rehearsal time. B–D are not supported; the performance is still ahead of the dancers.

RC.q: In [¶4], “making invisible movement visible” means the chalk drawing:
c: allowed dancers to move without being seen
glowed when the hall lights were turned off
represented planned motion on the ground
RC.e: The circles and arrows represented motion before it happened. A and B interpret invisible literally, while D confuses planning with recording.

RC.q: How does the author organize the middle of the passage?
c: By comparing four different choreographers and their styles
By describing the plan, the problem, and Suri's revision
By listing the rules for using a public basketball court
By arguing that dancers should always rehearse alone
RC.e: [¶2–¶3] moves from drawing the map to discovering a collision and revising a path. The other structures are absent.

RC.q: Which choice best connects the roof's function with the students' investigation?
c: Students discover that every school bus shelter should be built of wood.
A leaking shelter roof creates a safety problem for waiting students.
A planted roof manages rainwater and teaches students about starting conditions.
The environmental club replaces the school's bus shelter after three storms.
RC.e: C combines the roof's function [¶2] with the students' learning [¶3–¶4]. A and D are unsupported—the club measured rather than rebuilt—and B mistakes delayed release for a leak.

RC.q: Why did the largest storm not fill the barrel the most?
c: Dry soil absorbed much of its rain.
Students emptied the barrel during the storm.
The plants blocked every drainage channel.
Strong wind blew the barrel onto its side.
RC.e: [¶3] states that dry conditions let the soil absorb much of the largest storm. B–D are not mentioned.

RC.q: Why will the club compare two shelters in spring?
c: To determine which shelter has more students waiting beneath it
To find out whether a bare metal roof can collect any rain
To prove that the planted shelter never becomes warm in spring
To isolate whether the planted roof is related to temperature
RC.e: Comparing planted and unplanted shelters provides a reference for the temperature question in [¶4]. A and B ask different questions; C claims proof before evidence.

RC.q: In [¶3], “runoff” most nearly means:
c: soil carried away by strong wind
water that flows off a surface
a test that ends too early
RC.e: The passage discusses rain leaving the roof through channels, so runoff is water flowing from a surface. A, C, and D do not fit the water-management context.

RC.q: Why does the author include the students' future temperature study in [¶4]?
c: To show that recording conditions can guide a new investigation
To prove that the school's rain barrel was installed incorrectly
To introduce a disagreement between two student science clubs
To explain why spring storms are heavier than winter storms
RC.e: [¶4] transfers the students' lesson about starting conditions to a new test. B–D are neither stated nor supported.

MA.q: A reading drive collected 4,608 books in spring and 2,795 in fall. How many books were collected altogether?
MA.e: 4,608 + 2,795 = 7,403; B and D reflect carrying errors, and C drops one thousand.

MA.q: What is 7/8 − 1/3?
MA.e: With denominator 24, 21/24 − 8/24 = 13/24. A subtracts denominators, B changes only the numerator, and D uses an incorrect common denominator.

MA.q: Six identical notebooks cost $4.75 each. What is the total cost?
MA.e: 4.75 × 6 = 28.50. A multiplies only the dollars (4 × 6 = 24) and appends the 75 cents, C swaps the cents digits of 28.50, and D rounds to $5 × 6 = $30 and then adds the 75 cents back.

MA.q: A printer places 945 cards equally into 15 boxes. How many cards are in each box?
MA.e: 945 ÷ 15 = 63 because 15 × 63 = 945; the other choices come from incomplete division or rounding.

MA.q: A 240-page book has illustrations on 35% of its pages. How many pages have illustrations?
MA.e: 0.35 × 240 = 84; A finds 30%, B finds one third approximately, and D finds 40%.

MA.q: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 54?
MA.e: Common factors include 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 18; 18 is greatest. B and C are common but not greatest, while D is a multiple.
1/4 + 2/3 = 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12, and whole parts total 5. The distractors add denominators or regroup incorrectly.

MA.q: Which fraction is equal to 0.625?
MA.e: 0.625 = 625/1000 = 5/8; A and C are nearby values, while D places the decimal incorrectly.

MA.q: Solve 5x + 7 = 42.
MA.e: Subtract 7 from both sides to get 5x = 35, then divide by 5 for x = 7. A divides 35 by the constant 7 instead of by 5, C follows a subtraction slip (42 − 7 taken as 45, giving 45 ÷ 5 = 9), and D adds 7 to 42 before dividing (49 ÷ 5).

MA.q: What is the value of 3x² − 5 when x = 4?
MA.e: 4² = 16, then 3 × 16 − 5 = 43. A squares after multiplying incorrectly, and B or C reflect arithmetic errors.

MA.q: Which expression is equivalent to 6(y + 3)?
MA.e: Multiply both terms by 6: 6y + 18. B fails to distribute to 3, while C and D combine unlike terms.

MA.q: Which inequality is equivalent to n/4 < 6?
MA.e: Multiplying both sides by positive 4 gives n < 24; B reverses the sign, and A or D use wrong operations.

MA.q: Two angles of a triangle measure 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
MA.e: Triangle angles total 180°; 180 − (48 + 67) = 65°. The distractors reflect addition or subtraction errors.

MA.q: A parallelogram has a base of 13 cm and a perpendicular height of 8 cm. What is its area?
MA.e: Area = base × perpendicular height = 13 × 8 = 104 cm². A uses perimeter-like addition, C multiplies incorrectly, and D doubles the area.

MA.q: A circular table has a diameter of 18 feet. What is its radius?
MA.e: Radius is half the diameter, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9 feet. A doubles, B repeats the diameter, and D divides by three.

MA.q: A storage box is 7 feet long, 4 feet wide, and 3 feet high. What is its volume?
MA.e: Volume = 7 × 4 × 3 = 84 cubic feet. B multiplies only length and width (7 × 4 = 28), while C and D first add all three dimensions (7 + 4 + 3 = 14) and then multiply by the height (14 × 3 = 42) or the length (14 × 7 = 98) instead of multiplying all three dimensions.

MA.q: A ribbon is 2.35 meters long. How many centimeters long is it?
MA.e: One meter is 100 centimeters, so 2.35 × 100 = 235 cm. A multiplies by 10, B makes no unit-size adjustment, and D multiplies by 10,000.

MA.q: A workshop begins at 3:40 p.m. and lasts 2 hours 35 minutes. When does it end?
MA.e: 3:40 + 2 hours = 5:40, plus 35 minutes = 6:15. The distractors omit time or fail to regroup 60 minutes.

MA.q: What is the mean of 12, 15, 17, 20, and 21?
MA.e: The sum is 85, and 85 ÷ 5 = 17. The other choices result from choosing a middle or dividing incorrectly.

MA.q: A fair spinner is numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability of spinning an even number?
MA.e: Four of eight outcomes—2, 4, 6, 8—are even, so 4/8 = 1/2. The distractors miscount favorable outcomes.

MA.q: The number of minutes spent practicing over seven days was 18, 24, 18, 30, 21, 18, and 27. What is the mode?
MA.e: Eighteen appears three times, more than any other value. A–C appear once and may be chosen from order or size rather than frequency.

MA.q: In which quadrant is the point (−5, −2)?
MA.e: A negative x-coordinate and negative y-coordinate place the point in Quadrant III. The others correspond to different sign pairs.

MA.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?
MA.e: Each vertex-to-opposite-side-midpoint axis gives one line, for 5 total. A understates, C doubles, and D ignores regularity.

MA.q: A 10-by-8-meter rectangular patio has a 3-by-2-meter rectangular garden removed from one corner. What is the remaining patio area?
MA.e: Full area is 80 m² and removed area is 6 m², leaving 74 m². D ignores the removal, while A and B subtract dimensions or the wrong area.
Multiply and divide first: 18 − 12 + 4 = 10. B or C change operation order, and D combines numbers without precedence.

MA.q: Which is the prime factorization of 180?
MA.e: 180 = 4 × 45 = 2² × 3² × 5, and all factors are prime. A, C, and D still contain composite factors.

MA.sk: fractions—fraction of a fraction in context
MA.q: A class uses 3/5 of 45 sheets of paper. Of the sheets used, 2/3 are blue. How many blue sheets are used?
MA.e: 3/5 of 45 is 27, and 2/3 of 27 is 18. D stops after the first fraction; A and B apply the fractions incorrectly.

MA.q: On a drawing, 1 centimeter represents 250 centimeters. A hallway measures 6 centimeters on the drawing. How long is the actual hallway in meters?
MA.e: 6 × 250 = 1,500 cm = 15 m. A misses a factor of ten, B adds scale values, and C converts centimeters incorrectly.

MA.q: Twelve of 30 survey responses chose option A. What percent chose option A?
MA.e: 12/30 = 2/5 = 40%. A uses the total as a percent, C reverses part and remainder, and D is unrelated.

MA.q: A train travels 156 miles in 3 hours at a constant speed. What is its speed?
MA.e: Speed = 156 ÷ 3 = 52 mph. B is a division error, C divides by two, and D multiplies instead of divides.

VR.q: ADAPTABLE most nearly means:
VR.e: Adaptable means able to adjust, so flexible is precise; the distractors describe privacy, age, or accuracy.

VR.q: BARREN most nearly means:
VR.e: Barren land produces little or nothing; the other choices concern location, population, or worth.

VR.q: COMMENCE most nearly means:
VR.e: Commence means to begin; compare and gather are different actions, while delay opposes beginning.

VR.q: METICULOUS most nearly means:
VR.e: Meticulous describes extremely careful attention to detail; the distractors describe luck, sound, or mood.

VR.q: ELATED most nearly means:
VR.e: Elated means extremely joyful; exhaustion, confusion, and readiness do not express happiness.

VR.q: FRUGAL most nearly means:
VR.e: Frugal means careful about spending, closest to thrifty; wealth and elegance are unrelated, and wasteful is the opposite.

VR.q: AMIABLE most nearly means:
VR.e: An amiable person is friendly and pleasant; the other choices describe size, commonness, or speed.

VR.q: HOSTILE most nearly means:
VR.e: Hostile means unfriendly or opposing; harmless weakens the meaning, while uncertain and distant are unrelated.

VR.q: LOFTY most nearly means:
VR.e: Lofty means very high or elevated; height does not require hollowness, heaviness, or completeness.

VR.q: JAGGED most nearly means:
VR.e: Jagged describes a rough, sharply uneven edge; polish, width, and strength are separate qualities.

VR.q: OMIT most nearly means:
VR.e: To omit something is to leave it out; complaining, hurrying, and wandering are unrelated actions.

VR.q: MEAGER most nearly means:
VR.e: Meager means too small in amount, so small is closest; balanced, fresh, and useful do not indicate a lack.

VR.q: TRANQUIL most nearly means:
VR.e: Tranquil means calm and peaceful; hidden, uncertain, and ordinary describe different qualities.

VR.q: PERIL most nearly means:
VR.e: Peril is serious danger; shelter may protect from peril, while journey and argument are not synonyms.

VR.q: RESTORE most nearly means:
VR.e: To restore is to return something to a good condition, often by repairing it; the other verbs do not express renewal.

VR.q: SINCERE most nearly means:
VR.e: Sincere words or feelings are genuine; skill, caution, and formality do not guarantee honesty.

VR.q: VANISH most nearly means:
VR.e: To vanish is to disappear from sight; shrinking and traveling may change appearance or location, while arrive is unrelated.

VR.q: The mystery's first chapter was ____, but the ending explained everything.
VR.e: But signals contrast with an ending that explained everything, so confusing fits; brief, complete, and familiar do not create that contrast.

VR.q: The sidewalk was still wet, so Milo stepped ____ around the puddles.
VR.e: Wet pavement and puddles call for cautious movement; the distractors do not address the risk.

VR.q: The two recipes called for exactly the same ingredients and steps; there was no ____ between them.
VR.e: Calling for exactly the same ingredients and steps means no difference; promise, distance, and purpose are not defined by the clue.

VR.q: Grandpa keeps his childhood drawings in a sealed box to ____ them for the family.
VR.e: A sealed box helps preserve, or protect, the drawings for the future; measuring, releasing, or coloring them does not explain keeping them safe.

VR.q: Mei returned each borrowed tool clean and on time, proving she was ____.
VR.e: Consistently caring for and returning borrowed items shows dependability; the other traits are unsupported.

VR.q: From the hilltop, the distant lighthouse looked so ____ that it seemed no larger than a pencil.
VR.e: Appearing pencil-sized supplies a size clue for tiny; brightness, strength, and loneliness are not established.

VR.q: Before signing the form, Luis paused to ____ every line.
VR.e: Reviewing a form logically comes before signing; folding, copying, or skipping lines does not check it.

VR.q: The critic's comments were firm but ____, offering clear ways to improve the play.
VR.e: Suggestions for improvement make criticism constructive; the distractors do not explain its usefulness.

VR.q: The detective tried to ____ the owner of the unlabeled suitcase by checking its contents.
VR.e: Examining contents can identify the owner; imitation, invitation, and warning do not solve the ownership question.

VR.q: The room looked plain at noon, yet candlelight made it appear warm and ____.
VR.e: Yet contrasts plainness with a positive atmosphere, so inviting fits; the other choices continue or add negative traits.

VR.q: The small nation wanted to write its own laws rather than follow another country's, so it declared itself ____.
VR.e: Wanting to make its own laws leads a nation to declare itself independent; official, distant, and cheerful do not follow from that goal.

VR.q: The fallen branch ____ the narrow trail, forcing hikers to climb around it.
VR.e: Having to climb around the branch shows that it blocked the trail; the other verbs do not cause the detour.

VR.q: Helmets are required at the bike park, but knee pads are ____; each rider chooses whether to wear them.
VR.e: Since each rider chooses, the knee pads are optional, in contrast with required helmets; costly, modern, and popular do not describe something left to choice.

VR.q: The path was ____: it curved so often that travelers could not see far ahead.
VR.e: Frequent curves define a winding path; slope, shade, and mud are not mentioned.

VR.q: At the end of the meeting, the secretary read the decisions aloud to ____ the group's agreement.
VR.e: Reading decisions aloud can confirm shared agreement; the other verbs oppose or delay that purpose.

VR.q: When the first plan failed, the team had to ____ a different approach.
VR.e: To adopt an approach is to choose and begin using it; the distractors mean dismantle, miss, or forecast.

VR.q: The model was imperfect; ____, it revealed where the bridge needed extra support.
VR.e: Nevertheless shows that the model was useful despite its flaw; the other transitions express comparison, alternative, or simultaneous time.

QR.q: Red and blue flags are hung in a ratio of 3:5. If 64 flags are hung, how many are red?
QR.e: Eight ratio parts make 64, so each is 8 and red is 3×8=24; 40 is blue, while 32 and 48 misuse the ratio.

QR.q: Six identical jars of paint cost $16.50. At the same rate, what do ten jars cost?
QR.e: One jar costs $2.75, so ten cost $27.50; the distractors add quantities or scale the price incorrectly.

QR.q: A tank is 7/10 full. Water equal to 2/5 of the tank's total capacity is used. What fraction of the tank remains filled?
QR.e: 2/5 of the tank = 4/10, so 7/10 − 4/10 = 3/10 remains. B subtracts the denominator 5 from the numerator 7 (2/10 = 1/5), C subtracts the numerator 2 without converting (7/10 − 2/10 = 5/10 = 1/2), and D adds 2/10 instead of subtracting (9/10).

QR.q: In a class of 40 students, 35% ride a bicycle to school. How many students is that?
QR.e: 35% of 40 is 0.35×40=14; the other values reflect nearby percentages or rounding.

QR.q: A display doubles the number of lights and adds one each round: 4, 9, 19, 39, .... How many lights appear next?
QR.e: 39×2+1=79; 78 omits the added one, while 59 and 80 use inconsistent rules.

QR.q: A librarian shelves an average of 28 books per day for five days. She shelves 103 books during the first four days. How many does she shelve on day five?
QR.e: The five-day total is 5×28=140, and 140−103=37; 28 repeats the mean and 140 is the total.

QR.q: A rectangular garden has perimeter 54 meters and length 16 meters. What is its width?
QR.e: Half the perimeter is 54 ÷ 2 = 27, so the width is 27 − 16 = 11. A reports only how much longer the length is than the width (16 − 11 = 5), B subtracts one length from the whole perimeter and halves what is left (54 − 16 = 38, then 19), and C subtracts both lengths but forgets to halve (54 − 32 = 22).

QR.q: A bag holds 5 yellow, 7 green, and 8 blue tiles. What is the probability of drawing a tile that is not blue?
QR.e: Twelve of 20 tiles are not blue, so 12/20=3/5; 2/5 is the blue probability and the others miscount colors.

QR.q: A theater charges a $6 service fee plus $4 per student. A group pays $50. How many students are in the group?
QR.e: 4s+6=50 gives 4s=44 and s=11; the distractors divide before removing the fee or add it.

QR.q: On a trail map, 2.5 centimeters represent 15 kilometers. How many kilometers do 7 centimeters represent?
QR.e: The scale is 15÷2.5=6 kilometers per centimeter, so 7×6=42; the distractors use additive or inverted scaling.

QR.q: Crew A packs 84 cartons in 7 hours. Crew B packs 99 cartons in 9 hours. How many more cartons per hour does Crew A pack?
QR.e: Crew A packs 12 per hour and Crew B 11, a difference of 1; other choices compare totals or partial rates.

QR.q: An artist triples every edge length of a cube-shaped model. How many times as great is the new volume?
QR.e: Volume scales in three dimensions, so 3×3×3=27; 3 and 9 apply linear or area scaling only.

QR.q: A warehouse divides about 4,086 bolts equally among 79 bins. Which is the best estimate of bolts per bin?
QR.e: 4,000÷80=50, close to the given values; the distractors contain place-value or divisor-as-answer errors.

QR.q: A game token starts at (−4,−1), moves 9 units right, then 6 units up. Where does it stop?
QR.e: Add 9 to x and 6 to y to get (5,5); the distractors reverse a direction, swap a change, or misadd.

QR.q: The ratio of adult volunteers to student volunteers is 2:7. If 81 people volunteer, how many are adults?
QR.e: Nine parts make 81, so each part is 9 and adults are 2×9=18; 63 is the student count.

QR.q: A backpack priced at $80 is discounted 15%. What is the sale price?
QR.e: The discount is $12, leaving $68; $12 is the discount itself and the other choices use incorrect percentages.

QR.q: Wren finishes before Xena, and Zane finishes after Xena. Yori's position is unknown. Which order could be correct from first to last?
QR.e: Only C preserves Wren before Xena before Zane; every distractor reverses at least one required relation.

QR.q: A fair spinner numbered 1 through 8 is spun 96 times. About how many spins should land on a number greater than 6?
QR.e: Two of eight outcomes qualify, so 1/4×96=24; the distractors miscount outcomes or use the complement.

QR.q: A rectangular photograph is enlarged so both its length and width double. How does its area change?
QR.e: Area has two dimensions, so the scale factor is 2×2=4; the distractors use linear, additive, or volume scaling.

QR.q: After spending 3/8 of her savings, Talia has $45 left. How much did she have before spending?
QR.e: The $45 is 5/8 of the original, so 45×8/5=$72; the distractors treat 45 as the spent part or add a fraction of 45.

QR.q: Of 30 club members, 18 play chess, 16 play table tennis, and 7 play both. How many play neither?
QR.e: At least one is 18+16−7=27, so 30−27=3 play neither; distractors double-count or omit the overlap.

QR.q: At sunrise the temperature is −6°C. By noon it is 9°C. By how many degrees did it rise?
QR.e: Moving from −6 to 0 is 6 degrees and then to 9 is 9 more, totaling 15; the distractors subtract absolute values or ignore the negative start.

QR.q: A costume uses one of 3 shirts, one of 4 pairs of pants, and one of 2 hats. How many different costumes are possible?
QR.e: Multiply the independent choices: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24. A adds the three numbers (3 + 4 + 2 = 9), B multiplies shirts by pants but then only adds the hats (12 + 2 = 14), and C multiplies the shirts by the sum of pants and hats (3 × 6 = 18).

QR.q: A printer places 1,756 labels into sheets of 15. How many labels are left after filling as many complete sheets as possible?
QR.e: 15×117=1,755, leaving 1 label; the distractors use digit sums or distance from a wrong multiple.

QR.q: Every dren is a vop, and no vop is a sal. Which statement must be true?
QR.e: Because all drens belong to the vop group and vops exclude sals, drens cannot be sals; the distractors reverse or invent existence claims.

QR.q: A mural is painted 2/9 on Monday and 1/3 on Tuesday. What fraction remains unpainted?
QR.e: 1/3=3/9, so 5/9 is painted and 4/9 remains; distractors report the painted part or add unlike denominators.

QR.sk: data reasoning—median after adding a value
QR.q: The recorded times are 2, 5, 9, 11, and 14 minutes. If a 20-minute time is added, what is the new median?
QR.e: With six values, average the middle two: (9+11)/2=10; the distractors choose one middle value or average the wrong pair.

QR.q: A square plaza has area 175 square meters. Which is the closest estimate of one side length?
QR.e: Since 13²=169 and 14²=196, √175 is about 13.2; the distractors are farther from the correct interval or endpoint.

QR.sk: spatial reasoning—surface area with excluded face
QR.q: A 4 m by 3 m by 2 m display box is painted on the top and four sides, but not the bottom. What area is painted?
QR.e: Top area is 12; side areas total 2(4×2)+2(3×2)=28; painted area is 40. The distractors omit the top, include the bottom, or find volume.

QR.q: A culture begins with 200 cells, grows 20%, and then grows 25% from the new amount. How many cells are there?
QR.e: 200×1.20=240 and 240×1.25=300; the distractors add percentages to the original or apply one increase only.

QR.q: Two angles together form a straight line. One angle is 4 times as large as the other. What is the measure of the larger angle?
QR.e: The two angles total 180° and make 5 equal parts, so the smaller is 180 ÷ 5 = 36° and the larger is 4 × 36 = 144°. A stops at the smaller angle, B divides 180 by 4 instead of 5, and C uses 90° as the total (4 × 18 = 72).

QR.q: Three workers assemble 72 kits in 4 hours at equal steady rates. How many kits can five workers assemble in 6 hours?
QR.e: Each worker makes 72÷3÷4=6 kits per hour; 5×6×6=180. The distractors scale only workers, only time, or both incorrectly.

QR.q: Set A is 6, 10, 12, 18. Set B is 4, 9, 15, 23. How much greater is Set B's range than Set A's range?
QR.e: Range A is 18−6=12 and range B is 23−4=19, so the difference is 7; distractors report a range or mis-subtract.

QR.q: A group buys 6 tickets at $(x+2) each and uses a $5 coupon. Which expression gives the final cost?
QR.e: 6(x+2)−5=6x+12−5=6x+7; the distractors fail to distribute, omit the coupon, or multiply only part of the price.

QR.q: A court is 30 m by 18 m. A runner completes 1 3/4 laps around it. How far does the runner travel?
QR.e: One lap is 2 × (30 + 18) = 96 m, and 1 3/4 × 96 = 168 m. A stops after one lap, B adds only one more 30 m side for the extra three-quarters of a lap (96 + 30 = 126), and C runs 1 1/2 laps instead of 1 3/4 (1.5 × 96 = 144).

QR.q: A box holds cards numbered 1 through 15. One card is drawn at random. What is the probability that the number drawn is greater than 9?
QR.e: The favorable cards are 10 through 15—six of the 15—so the probability is 6/15 = 2/5. A counts the nine cards that are 9 or less (9/15 = 3/5), B wrongly includes the 9 itself (7/15), and D drops one favorable card (5/15 = 1/3).

QR.q: After a 30% discount, a lamp costs $63. What was its original price?
QR.e: The sale price is 70% of the original, so 63÷0.70=90; the distractors add 30% of the sale price or use incorrect bases.

QR.q: Parcel P is heavier than parcel Q. Parcel R is lighter than parcel Q. Which statement must be true?
c: P and R have equal weight.
QR.e: The chain P>Q>R guarantees P>R; every distractor reverses or contradicts that chain.

RC.q: Which summary best captures the ferry-signal passage?
c: Simple signals made ferry trips more efficient.
The bending river became impossible to cross.
The shop owner built the first permanent bridge.
Freight mattered more to the ferry than passengers.
RC.e: The problem, signal system, and reduced unnecessary crossings support A; the other choices exaggerate, invent construction, or make an unsupported comparison.

RC.q: What did a white square signal?
c: The river was too foggy for boats.
The new bridge was open at last.
RC.e: S3 directly assigns white to freight; C is the red signal, while A and B are not flag meanings.

RC.q: Why was a bell useful during fog?
c: It counted every crate waiting on the landing.
It frightened the animals waiting on the bank.
Sound could carry when the flags could not be seen.
It announced that the bridge was finally done.
RC.e: S5 contrasts invisible flags with bell patterns, supporting C; the distractors assign functions the passage never gives.

RC.q: In S6, “unnecessary” most nearly means:
RC.e: Better information prevented trips that were not needed; danger, cost, and completion are not the stated issue.

RC.q: Which sequence best describes the author's organization of the Silverbend passage?
c: A long debate followed by a final vote
Two rival ferrymen compared in careful detail
A numbered list of rules for crossing the river
A problem, a solution, a limit, and a result
RC.e: The bend creates a problem, flags solve it, fog limits them, and records show a result; the other structures do not match the sequence.

RC.q: Which summary best captures the fog-collector passage?
c: Fog collectors work everywhere without maintenance.
Mesh panels can collect useful water in suitable places.
Covered tanks create the fog that drifts over hills.
Strong winds always improve the water collected.
RC.e: B includes both the method and its conditions; A and D ignore limitations, while C reverses the process.

RC.q: What happens after droplets join into larger drops?
c: They turn into salt and dust.
They rise upward through the pipe.
They tear holes in the mesh.
RC.e: S3 states that larger drops slide into a channel; the other choices reverse motion or confuse problems with steps.

RC.q: Why do designers study local wind direction?
c: To leave the water tank uncovered outdoors
To stop salt and dust from ever forming
To be sure moving fog blows through the mesh
To change salty seawater into fresh drinking water
RC.e: Collection depends on wind pushing fog through mesh, so site direction matters; the distractors invent unrelated effects.

RC.q: Why does the author mention torn or blocked mesh?
c: To show practical limits that require planning
To argue that fog never contains any water
To explain how the covered storage tanks are built
To prove that rain falls more often than fog
RC.e: Those examples qualify the method and motivate site study; the other choices contradict or leave the passage.

RC.q: In S8, “suitable” most nearly means:
RC.e: Suitable places have appropriate wind, weather, and conditions; the other adjectives are not supported.

RC.q: What does Inez learn by the end?
c: Every window box should look perfectly neat.
Clubs work best when they avoid making plans.
A plan can guide people without rigid divisions.
Feeding birds matters more than any other goal.
RC.e: S9 states the flexible-plan insight; A, B, and D turn a balanced lesson into an extreme claim.

RC.q: What did Inez place in the empty box?
RC.e: S5 directly names three paper squares; the distractors name planting-day objects the passage never places in the box or ideas that come later.

RC.q: Why had the club's box remained empty?
c: Members waited for a plan that satisfied competing goals.
The spring festival had been canceled before planting day.
Inez had lost all of the club's flower seeds.
The community center forbade berries and blossoms.
RC.e: The disagreement and desire for a complete plan delayed action; the distractors invent events or rules.

RC.q: What lesson does the window-box episode best support?
c: The neatest window box is always the most useful.
Combining purposes helps a group move past disagreement.
A successful group must agree on one single goal.
A nature project should never use written labels.
RC.e: The group succeeds by combining food, color, and habitat; the other choices reverse or overstate the lesson.

RC.q: What does “sharp borders” in S7 suggest?
c: Dangerous edges on the wooden box
Brightly painted lines on the soil
Small fences around the whole center
RC.e: The sections represent purposes, and one plant can cross categories; the other choices interpret borders physically without support.

RC.q: What central idea does the passage develop?
c: Every faded mural should be completely repainted in bright color.
Careful restoration balances clarity with honesty about gaps.
Infrared light permanently changes the mural's pigments.
The new paint is weaker than the wall's old plaster.
RC.e: The team's limited, distinguishable repairs support B; the other choices contradict or focus on an unsupported technical claim.

RC.q: What did the team do before adding repairs?
c: Covered the whole mural with fresh plaster
Asked viewers to guess the missing scene
Photographed the wall and cleaned a test area
Repainted every missing shape in new color
RC.e: S3-S5 give photography and test cleaning before repair; A and D reverse the work, while B is never done.

RC.q: Why were the new marks kept visible when viewed up close?
c: So viewers could tell repairs from original paint
Because the team ran out of matching paint
So infrared cameras could find the buried mural
Because people standing close cannot see faded color
RC.e: Distinguishability avoids pretending uncertain repairs are original; the distractors invent material limits or misuse infrared.

RC.q: In S5, “supported” most nearly means:
RC.e: Hidden outlines provide evidence for a pattern, so supported means backed by evidence; the other choices use literal or unrelated senses.

RC.q: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
c: A beautiful guess is worth as much as real historical evidence.
Every missing detail should be left impossible for anyone to see.
Restoration should aid understanding without hiding uncertainty.
Modern tools such as infrared make careful judgment unnecessary.
RC.e: The final choice combines understanding and honesty; the distractors reject evidence, usefulness, or expert judgment.

RC.q: Which summary best captures the library's new lending project?
c: A library should stop lending books and recordings.
Every household should buy its own drill and telescope.
Shared objects never break and never need new parts.
A library adapted its rules so objects could be shared safely.
RC.e: D captures the expansion and safeguards; the other choices contradict the passage or make absolute claims.

RC.q: Why did staff photograph each kit before checkout?
c: To advertise the new kits to residents
To teach borrowers how to take photographs
To record the kit's parts and condition
To shorten the waiting list for popular kits
RC.e: Photographs and labels support inspection and complete returns; the distractors give unrelated purposes.

RC.q: What did the waiting list help the staff infer?
c: Which library books should be removed
Which residents already owned their own tools
RC.e: A long wait signals demand and helps guide purchases; the distractors concern information the list does not contain.

RC.q: Why did the library allow extra time between object loans?
c: The objects were less popular than the library's books.
Borrowers needed extra time to buy replacements.
Staff needed to inspect the objects and parts.
The library building closed between every loan.
RC.e: Different objects and labeled parts required inspection; the distractors invent low demand, borrower duties, or closures.

RC.q: What lesson does the library-of-things project best support?
c: Sharing succeeds when the rules match what is shared.
Careful rules always prevent shared objects from breaking.
People should borrow everything they use at home.
Predictions about new library projects are never useful.
RC.e: The library adapts rules and succeeds with manageable repairs; the other choices use absolutes that the passage does not support.

MA.e: Place-value addition gives 9,803; the distractors reflect regrouping or place-value slips.
Regrouping across zeros gives 4,416; the distractors reverse digits or subtract without regrouping.

MA.q: What is 74×36?
MA.e: 74×(30+6)=2,220+444=2,664; the distractors contain partial-product errors.

MA.q: What is 2,916÷27?
MA.e: 27×108=2,916; the distractors reflect quotient-estimation or place-value errors.
Using denominator 36 gives 10/36+21/36=31/36; the distractors add denominators or convert only one fraction.

MA.q: What is 5/6−7/20?
MA.e: 5/6=50/60 and 7/20=21/60, so the difference is 29/60; the distractors subtract denominators or use a wrong common denominator.
Cancel 8/32 to 1/4 and 25/15 to 5/3, giving 5/12; the distractors add, over-cancel, or combine denominators incorrectly.

MA.q: What is 3 1/3÷5/6?
MA.e: 10/3×6/5=4; the distractors fail to invert the divisor or mishandle the mixed number.
Align decimals: 18.709+6.840=25.549; the distractors misalign places or regroup incorrectly.

MA.q: What is 4.8×2.35?
MA.e: 235×48=11,280, then place three decimal digits to get 11.28; the distractors misplace the decimal or add.
Scale to 277.2÷42=6.6; the distractors move the decimal the wrong number of places or estimate poorly.

MA.q: What is 22% of 450?
MA.e: 20% of 450 is 90 and 2% is 9, totaling 99; the distractors omit a part or misplace the decimal.
Parentheses first: 42÷7=6 and 5×2=10, then 6+10=16; distractors ignore grouping or multiplication priority.

MA.q: What is 5^3?
MA.e: 5^3=5×5×5=125; the distractors multiply base by exponent, square, or use the fourth power.

MA.q: Which is the prime factorization of 126?
MA.e: 126=2×3×3×7, all prime; every distractor leaves composite factors.

MA.q: What is the greatest common factor of 48 and 72?
MA.e: 24 divides both and no larger common factor does; 12 and 8 are common but not greatest, while 144 is a multiple.

MA.q: Solve 6x−11=43.
MA.e: Add 11 to get 6x=54, then divide by 6 to get x=9; the distractors stop early or undo operations incorrectly.

MA.q: What is 2c²+3c when c=4?
MA.e: 2(4²)+3(4)=32+12=44; the distractors square the coefficient or apply the exponent to the whole expression.

MA.q: Which value of n satisfies 3n−5≥16?
MA.e: For n=7, 3n−5=16, which satisfies ≥; the smaller choices produce values below 16.

MA.q: What is the reflection of (−3,8) across the y-axis?
MA.e: A y-axis reflection changes the sign of x only; the distractors reflect across x, swap coordinates, or change both signs.

MA.q: A parallelogram has base 14 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. What is its area?
MA.e: Area is base×height=14×9=126 cm²; the distractors find perimeter-like totals, halve, or double the product.

MA.q: A triangle has angles of 52° and 61°. What is the third angle?
MA.e: Triangle angles total 180°, so 180 − (52 + 61) = 180 − 113 = 67°. D stops at the sum of the two given angles (113°), while A and C come from misadding 52 + 61 (as 123 or 103) before subtracting from 180°.

MA.q: Using 22/7 for π, what is the circumference of a circle with radius 7 cm?
MA.e: Circumference=2πr=2×(22/7)×7=44 cm; the distractors use half the formula or compute area.

MA.q: What is the volume of a rectangular prism measuring 8 cm by 6 cm by 5 cm?
MA.e: Volume = 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 cm³. A finds only the top and bottom faces (2 × 48 = 96), and B and C are slips in the final step 48 × 5: misreading 48 as 38 gives 190, and taking 200 + 4 × 5 instead of 200 + 8 × 5 gives 220.

MA.q: How many milliliters are in 4.25 liters?
MA.e: One liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 4.25×1,000=4,250; the distractors move the decimal the wrong number of places.

MA.q: How much time passes from 1:47 p.m. to 4:15 p.m.?
MA.e: From 1:47 to 2:00 is 13 minutes, to 4:00 is 2 hours, and to 4:15 is 15 minutes: 2 h 28 min. Distractors subtract minute digits directly.

MA.q: On a drawing, 1.5 cm represents 6 m. What actual distance does 8 cm represent?
MA.e: The scale is 6÷1.5=4 m per cm, so 8×4=32 m; the distractors use additive or inverted scaling.

MA.q: What is the mean of 18, 23, 27, 32, and 40?
MA.e: The sum is 140, and 140÷5=28; the distractors choose a middle value or divide incorrectly.

MA.q: A card numbered 1 through 20 is chosen at random. What is the probability that its number is a factor of 18?
MA.e: Factors within the set are 1,2,3,6,9,18: 6/20=3/10; the distractors omit factors or count multiples.

MA.q: How far apart are points (−4,2) and (−4,−7)?
MA.e: The x-coordinates match, and vertical distance is |2−(−7)|=9; the distractors subtract absolute values or add coordinates incorrectly.

calendar.note: Researched from official E3n (formerly ERB) pages and Seattle-area school admissions pages. Plan weeks and mocks are added by the app from the study plan. Day-level season boundaries are inferred from the official month ranges.

level.name: ISEE Lower Level
level.order: Verbal Reasoning 34 q / 20 min → Quantitative Reasoning 38 q / 35 min → break 10 min → Reading Comprehension 25 q / 25 min → Mathematics Achievement 30 q / 30 min → break 10 min → Essay 30 min
level.total: 127 questions + essay · 2 h 20 min of testing plus two 10-minute breaks
level.rule: Students may take the ISEE once per testing season — Fall, Winter, and Spring/Summer — for a total of up to three times a school year.

formats.name: Prometric test center
formats.detail: Online, grades 5–12. Seattle-area center is in Mountlake Terrace (nothing in Bellevue). Pick a date in Prometric's scheduler; a parent must stay at the center for the whole test. Fee $250. Change/cancel: free 31+ days out, $25 at 30–15 days, $45 at 14–5 days, $75 at 4–1 days.

formats.name: ISEE at Home
formats.detail: Online and proctored, offered most days; needs two camera devices (test device + phone/tablet). Fee $250, or $170 when a member school proctors. Reschedule $50, cancel $55.

formats.name: School test site
formats.detail: Group sitting at an independent school, paper or online. $170 standard; late (14–20 days before) $215; walk-in (under 13 days) $230. Online sittings can be booked up to 3 days before, paper sittings 21+ days before.

scores.detail: Online tests (Prometric, at-home, online school sites): scores usually ready in 3–5 days; paper: 5–10 days. Choose which schools receive scores at registration or after seeing them; only complete reports can be sent.

events.title: ISEE Fall testing season
events.detail: One sitting allowed in this season. Portal label: “2026 Fall”.

events.title: ISEE Winter testing season
events.detail: One sitting allowed in this season. Portal label: “2026-27 Winter”. A December date still lands before the January application deadlines.

events.title: ISEE Spring/Summer testing season
events.detail: Third and last possible sitting of the cycle — after most fall-2027 application deadlines.

events.title: ISEE at The Bush School (Seattle)
events.detail: Saturday group sitting for applicants to grades 5–12. Register through the ISEE portal.

events.detail: Closed on-campus session, grades 6–12. Registration code 447JKHUW.

events.title: Book the real ISEE by early December

2026-09.text: Decide how Sheila will sit the real ISEE — Prometric (Mountlake Terrace), at home, or a school sitting — and pin the target date on the Calendar
2026-09.why: Everything else (registration cutoffs, score timing) hangs off this.

2026-09.text: Run the split diagnostic (Sep 21–27): Part A one day, Part B another, real timing
Set up the mock-exam spot: quiet room, scratch paper, no notes, clock visible
2026-09.why: Mocks only predict the real day if the conditions match.

2026-09.text: Rate the Week-1 precision words she already wrote (they show 'Needs a rating')
2026-09.why: Ratings decide what goes back into review.

2026-10.text: If using the Bush School group sitting (Sat Oct 24), register through the ISEE portal early in the month
Mock 1 (Oct 19–25), then the correction week (Oct 26–Nov 1): classify every miss, reteach, redo
Collect the ISEE school codes for the target schools (e.g. Lakeside 481120, Overlake 480073, Bear Creek 481705)

2026-11.text: If using the Eastside Catholic sitting (Sat Dec 5), register by Fri Nov 20 with code 447JKHUW
If not using a school sitting, book Prometric or ISEE at Home now — Lakeside asks families to register by December
2026-11.why: Slots fill in December; scores take 3–5 days after an online test.

2026-11.text: Mock 3 final rehearsal (Nov 23–29), full length in one sitting
Week before the test: normal bedtimes, light review only, no new material

Scores arrive in 3–5 days (online) — choose which schools receive them; adding schools is free
Confirm every target school is on the score-recipient list before the January deadlines

books.note: Independent reading. The starter books are what Sheila has actually read or is reading; suggestions are well-known middle-grade titles chosen for the reading skills the ISEE tests. A starter book added later is put on the shelf by seedBooks on every device, once.

starter.title: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone
starter.author: J. K. Rowling
starter.note: MinaLima illustrated edition · started at chapter 5

suggestions.title: The Secret Garden
suggestions.author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
suggestions.why: Older, formal language and long descriptive passages — closest thing to an ISEE reading passage.

suggestions.title: Anne of Green Gables
suggestions.author: L. M. Montgomery
suggestions.why: Rich figurative language and a big vocabulary; a natural next step if she likes Little Women.

suggestions.title: The Westing Game
suggestions.author: Ellen Raskin
suggestions.why: A puzzle mystery — nothing is stated outright, so it is pure inference practice.

suggestions.title: Holes
suggestions.author: Louis Sachar
suggestions.why: Three timelines braided together; good for questions about how a text is organised.

suggestions.title: Number the Stars
suggestions.author: Lois Lowry
suggestions.why: Historical fiction: context clues and tone carry most of the meaning.

suggestions.title: Because of Winn-Dixie
suggestions.author: Kate DiCamillo
suggestions.why: Short chapters, and almost every feeling is implied rather than stated.

suggestions.title: Where the Mountain Meets the Moon
suggestions.author: Grace Lin
suggestions.why: Folktales nested inside a story — main idea and theme practice.

suggestions.title: A Wrinkle in Time
suggestions.author: Madeleine L'Engle
suggestions.why: Abstract ideas and harder vocabulary; a real step up.

suggestions.title: Wonder
suggestions.author: R. J. Palacio
suggestions.why: Several narrators tell the same events — point of view practice.

suggestions.title: The Wild Robot
suggestions.author: Peter Brown
suggestions.why: Plain sentences and strong cause and effect; an easy, enjoyable one between harder books.

aops.note: Where each ISEE maths skill is taught in the AoPS material. Beast Academy references are level + unit as published on beastacademy.com; Prealgebra references are chapter titles from the AoPS Prealgebra contents (the book numbers chapters, but titles are stable across printings). Alcumus and the Prealgebra video series are free with an AoPS account.
